sections.title: Inversion and fronting
sections.summary: Moving a negative or restrictive adverbial to the front of a clause forces the auxiliary in front of the subject: 'Never have I seen such a thing.' This chapter covers the full set of triggers, the mechanics of inversion and the fronting patterns that do not invert, all of which mark formal, rhetorically controlled English.

rules.title: Negative and restrictive adverbials trigger subject–auxiliary inversion
rules.body: When a clause opens with a negative or restrictive adverbial such as never, rarely, seldom, little, nowhere, at no time, under no circumstances, on no account or in no way, the auxiliary (or be) moves in front of the subject, exactly as in a question: 'Rarely has a decision been so badly timed.' The fronted phrase must be negative or restrictive in meaning, not merely fronted: 'In some respects he was right' takes no inversion. The structure belongs to formal or rhetorical registers; in casual conversation it can sound stilted.

examples.target: Never have I been so insulted.
examples.en: fronted never, have inverted before the subject

examples.target: Under no circumstances should the door be left unlocked.
examples.en: fronted negative prepositional phrase with modal inversion

examples.target: Little did she realise what awaited her.
examples.en: little = 'not at all'; dummy did inserted

examples.target: At no time were the passengers in danger.

rules.title: Not only ... but (also)
rules.body: 'Not only' at the start of a clause triggers inversion in that clause only; the second clause keeps normal order: 'Not only did he refuse, but he also insulted the host.' Pair it with 'but', 'but also', or 'but ... as well'; a semicolon can replace 'but'. Inversion does not occur when 'not only' modifies a noun phrase inside the clause rather than the clause itself: 'Not only the staff but also the guests were evacuated.'

examples.target: Not only did the plan fail, but it also cost us a client.
examples.en: inversion in the first clause only

examples.target: Not only is she a gifted pianist; she also composes.
Not only the roof but also the walls were damaged.
examples.en: not only modifies a noun phrase: no inversion

rules.title: No sooner ... than; hardly, scarcely, barely ... when
rules.body: These pairs describe one event following immediately on another. The first clause is usually in the past perfect with inversion, the second in the past simple: 'No sooner had we sat down than the phone rang.' 'No sooner' is a comparative, so it takes 'than'; 'hardly', 'scarcely' and 'barely' take 'when' (or 'before'). Mixing them (*no sooner ... when) is a common error even among native speakers.

examples.target: No sooner had the curtain risen than the lights failed.
examples.en: no sooner ... than, past perfect inverted

examples.target: Hardly had I closed the door when the bell rang.
Scarcely had the ink dried before the contract was challenged.

rules.title: Only + adverbial: invert in the main clause
rules.body: 'Only when', 'only after', 'only if', 'only by', 'only then', 'only later', 'only in this way' and similar phrases cause inversion, but when 'only' introduces a subordinate clause, the inversion falls on the main clause that follows it, not on the only-clause: 'Only when the results came in did we understand.' Compare 'Only then did I realise', where 'only then' is a simple adverbial and inversion is immediate.

examples.target: Only after the audit was complete did the board act.
examples.en: subordinate clause first, main clause inverted

examples.target: Only by listening carefully can you hear the difference.
Only then did the truth emerge.
Only if you sign today will the discount apply.

rules.title: Not until, not since, not for
rules.body: 'Not until' and 'not since' behave like 'only when': the inversion falls on the main clause after the subordinate clause or phrase: 'Not until the last page is the murderer revealed.' The same applies to 'not for' + a period of time: 'Not for a moment did I doubt her.' These are stronger, more deliberate alternatives to the cleft 'It wasn't until ... that', treated in chapter 2.

examples.target: Not until I saw the bill did I grasp the cost.
examples.en: not until + clause, main clause inverted

examples.target: Not since the war has the town seen such crowds.
examples.en: not since + noun, present perfect inverted

examples.target: Not for one moment did he consider resigning.

rules.title: So + adjective/adverb ... that; such + be + noun
rules.body: A fronted 'so' + adjective (or adverb) inverts the clause and is followed by a that-clause of result: 'So fierce was the storm that the bridge closed.' 'Such' can be fronted on its own before 'be': 'Such was the noise that nobody heard the alarm.' Both are literary or journalistic; the everyday equivalents are 'The storm was so fierce that ...' and 'The noise was such that ...'.

examples.target: So loud was the music that the neighbours complained.
So quickly did events unfold that the press could not keep up.
Such was her confidence that she declined to rehearse.

rules.title: How inversion is built
rules.body: Inversion moves only the first auxiliary: 'Never has he been asked' (not *Never has been he asked). If the verb has no auxiliary, insert do/does/did and leave the main verb in its base form: 'Seldom does she complain'; 'Rarely did they win.' 'Be' as a main verb inverts directly: 'Nowhere is this clearer.' Modals and perfect 'have' invert like other auxiliaries: 'Under no circumstances may you leave'; 'Little had they expected it.'

examples.target: Seldom does a week pass without a complaint.
examples.en: no auxiliary: does inserted, main verb in base form

examples.target: Never has so much been owed by so many to so few.
Nowhere is the gap wider than in housing.
Rarely could a candidate have been less prepared.
examples.en: modal inverts; have been stays in place

rules.title: Nor, neither and so: agreement and addition
rules.body: After a negative statement, a clause beginning with 'nor' or 'neither' inverts: 'She didn't apply, nor did her brother.' After an affirmative, 'so' + auxiliary + subject adds agreement: 'He plays chess, and so does his daughter.' The auxiliary must match the tense and form of the first clause (so do I / so did I / so have I / so am I). Chapter 10 returns to these as substitution devices.

examples.target: I have never liked opera, nor has my wife.
examples.en: nor + has, matching the present perfect

examples.target: The first bid was rejected, and so was the second.
She can't swim, and neither can he.

rules.title: Fronting without inversion, and inversion of the full verb
rules.body: Fronting for emphasis or contrast does not always invert. An object or complement can move to the front with normal subject–verb order: 'This I cannot accept'; 'Beautiful it was not.' With adverbials of place or direction and verbs of position or movement (be, stand, lie, come, go, hang, walk), the whole verb moves in front of a noun subject: 'On the hill stood a ruined chapel'; 'Here comes the bus.' With a pronoun subject there is no inversion: 'Here it comes.'

examples.target: This we can agree on.
At the foot of the stairs lay a bundle of letters.
examples.en: place adverbial + full verb + noun subject

examples.target: Here comes the train. / Here it comes.
examples.en: noun subject inverts, pronoun subject does not

examples.target: In walked the manager, unannounced.

rules.title: Had, were, should: the fronted auxiliary of condition
rules.body: A conditional clause can drop 'if' and front its auxiliary: 'Had I known, I would have called' (= If I had known); 'Were she here, she would object'; 'Should you need help, ring this number.' Only had, were and should invert in this way, and the negative is not contracted: 'Had it not been for ...', not *Hadn't it been. Chapter 3 treats the full range of these forms.

examples.target: Had I known, I would have called.
Were the offer genuine, we would accept.
Should you require assistance, please ask.

exercises.q: Never ___ such a mess.
exercises.explain: After fronted 'never', the auxiliary 'have' moves in front of the subject.

exercises.q: After 'Not only ...', the second clause introduced by 'but' also takes inversion.
exercises.explain: Only the not-only clause inverts; the but-clause keeps normal subject–verb order.

exercises.q: Rewrite with inversion: 'I had no sooner sat down than the phone rang.' → No sooner ___ sat down than the phone rang. (two words)
exercises.explain: Fronted 'no sooner' moves the auxiliary 'had' in front of the subject.

exercises.q: Hardly had the meeting started ___ the fire alarm went off.
exercises.explain: 'Hardly' pairs with 'when'; 'than' belongs with the comparative 'no sooner'.

exercises.answer: Seldom does he admit that he was wrong.
exercises.en: He rarely admits being wrong (fronted seldom with dummy does).

exercises.q: Rarely ___ a film received such unanimous praise. (auxiliary)
exercises.explain: Present perfect 'has received' inverts to 'has a film received'.

exercises.q: 'Only after the audit was completed did the board act' is correctly inverted.
exercises.explain: With 'only after' + clause, the inversion falls on the main clause, as here.

exercises.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: Only when did she arrive we could start.
Only when she arrived could we start.
Only when she arrived we could start.
Only when did she arrive could we start.
exercises.explain: The only-clause keeps normal order; the main clause inverts ('could we start').

exercises.q: Little ___ they know that the house had already been sold. (auxiliary)
exercises.explain: 'Little' is a negative adverb; with no auxiliary present, 'did' is inserted.

exercises.answer: Not until the final whistle did the crowd relax.
exercises.en: The crowd relaxed only at the final whistle.

exercises.q: So ___ that nobody recognised him.
exercises.explain: The adjective goes with 'so' at the front, then 'be' inverts with the subject.

exercises.q: 'In some ways was he right' is a correct use of inversion.
exercises.explain: 'In some ways' is neither negative nor restrictive, so there is no inversion: 'In some ways he was right.'

exercises.q: Rewrite: 'The noise was such that nobody heard the alarm.' → ___ was the noise that nobody heard the alarm.
exercises.explain: Fronted 'such' is followed directly by inverted 'be'.

pairs: Not only the staff but also the guests ...
no inversion: not only modifies a noun phrase
full-verb inversion with a noun subject

exercises.q: She has never liked opera, ___.
exercises.explain: 'Nor' inverts and the auxiliary must match the present perfect of the first clause.

exercises.q: Nowhere ___ the problem more visible than in the capital. (form of 'be')
exercises.explain: Main-verb 'be' inverts directly after fronted 'nowhere'.

exercises.answer: Under no circumstances should these files leave the building.
exercises.en: These files must never leave the building.

exercises.q: In 'Had I known about the delay, I would have left earlier', 'had' replaces 'if'.
exercises.explain: Fronting 'had' is the formal equivalent of 'If I had known'.

exercises.q: Rewrite without 'if': 'If you should need further details, contact us.' → ___ you need further details, contact us.
exercises.explain: 'Should' is fronted and 'if' dropped.

exercises.q: Which fronted phrase does NOT trigger inversion?
exercises.explain: 'In most cases' is not negative or restrictive, so the clause keeps normal order.

exercises.q: Not since the floods ___ the river risen so high. (auxiliary)
exercises.explain: 'Not since' + noun inverts the following clause: 'has the river risen'.

exercises.answer: So quickly did the news spread that the switchboard was jammed.
exercises.en: The news spread so quickly that the switchboard was jammed.

exercises.q: 'Not only did he apologise, but he also offered to pay' is correct.
exercises.explain: Inversion in the not-only clause, normal order after 'but'.

exercises.q: Spot the error.
options: No sooner had she left than it started to rain.
Hardly had we arrived when the show began.
No sooner had he spoken when he regretted it.
Scarcely had the ink dried before the deal collapsed.
exercises.explain: 'No sooner' is a comparative and must be followed by 'than', not 'when'.

exercises.q: Rewrite with fronting and inversion: 'I did not doubt her for a moment.' → Not for a moment ___ her. (three words)
exercises.explain: 'Not for' + period fronts, so 'did' is inserted and the main verb stays in the base form.

pairs: Such was the heat that the rails buckled.
full-verb inversion after a direction adverbial

exercises.q: Rewrite with inversion: 'It was only by sheer luck that we escaped.' → Only by sheer luck ___ escape. (two words)
exercises.explain: 'Only by' + phrase inverts the clause immediately, with dummy 'did'.

exercises.q: 'Rarely has been a candidate so unprepared' is correctly formed.
exercises.explain: Only the first auxiliary moves: 'Rarely has a candidate been so unprepared.'

exercises.answer: At the end of the lane stood a small white cottage.
exercises.en: A small white cottage stood at the end of the lane (full-verb inversion).

sections.title: Cleft and emphatic structures
sections.summary: Clefts split one proposition into two clauses so that a single element carries the focus: 'It was the price that put me off'; 'What I need is time.' This chapter covers it-clefts, wh-clefts and their reversed forms, 'the reason why' and 'all' clefts, and emphatic 'do', with attention to agreement and formal usage.

rules.title: It-clefts: It was X that/who ...
rules.body: An it-cleft places the focused element after 'it + be' and puts the rest of the sentence in a that-clause: 'It was Tom who broke the vase.' Any element except the verb can be focused: subject, object, adverbial of time, place or manner. 'That' is the default link; 'who' is common for people, 'when' and 'where' are possible for time and place in informal style. The tense of 'be' usually matches the clause: 'It was in 2010 that we met.'

examples.target: It was the price that put me off, not the quality.
It was in Lisbon that we first met.
It is you who are to blame.
examples.en: focus on a pronoun; verb agrees with you

examples.target: It wasn't until midnight that the votes were counted.

rules.title: Wh-clefts (pseudo-clefts): What I need is ...
rules.body: A wh-cleft begins with a what-clause acting as subject, followed by 'be' and the focused element: 'What I need is a holiday.' The what-clause takes a singular verb, though a plural complement allows a plural: 'What I need are two volunteers.' With 'do', the action itself is focused and the complement is a bare or to-infinitive: 'What she did was (to) resign.' 'What happened was that ...' focuses an entire event.

examples.target: What I need is a quiet weekend.
examples.en: what-clause as subject, focus on a noun phrase

examples.target: What she did next was call the police.
What happened was that the server crashed.
examples.en: whole event focused in a that-clause

rules.title: Reversed wh-clefts
rules.body: The two halves of a wh-cleft can be swapped so that the focused element comes first and the what-clause follows: 'A holiday is what I need'; 'That is what I meant.' Reversed clefts often pick up a demonstrative ('this', 'that') and are very common in speech for summing up or agreeing. They are also used with 'the reason', 'the place' and 'where': 'Here is where it all began.'

examples.target: Time is what we lack.
That is exactly what I was afraid of.
Money is what matters to them.
examples.en: reversed cleft with what as subject of its clause

rules.title: The reason why ..., the place where ..., the thing that ...
rules.body: Nouns such as reason, place, time, thing, person and way can head a cleft-like structure: 'The reason why we failed was that we started late.' In formal writing the complement after 'the reason ... is' should be 'that', not 'because', which many editors regard as redundant. 'The thing that' and 'the person who' are informal alternatives to what-clefts and it-clefts respectively.

examples.target: The reason why the launch was postponed was that the tests failed.
The place where we first met has been demolished.
examples.en: noun + relative clause as a focusing frame

examples.target: The thing that impresses me most is her honesty.

rules.title: All-clefts: All I want is ...
rules.body: 'All' + clause + 'be' works like a what-cleft but adds the meaning 'nothing more than': 'All I want is a cup of tea.' With 'do', the complement is normally a bare infinitive: 'All he did was laugh.' A to-infinitive is also possible and slightly more formal. The structure is a compact way to minimise or dismiss.

examples.target: All I want is a cup of tea.
All he did was nod.
All we can do now is wait.
examples.en: all + modal clause + be + bare infinitive

rules.title: Emphatic do
rules.body: In affirmative statements and imperatives, 'do/does/did' can be inserted before the main verb and stressed to confirm, contradict or insist: 'I do like it'; 'She did warn you'; 'Do sit down.' It is used for contrast with an expectation ('You never call.' 'I do call!'), for polite insistence in invitations, and to reinforce a point in argument. The main verb stays in the base form.

examples.target: I did warn you about the traffic.
examples.en: stressed did confirming a past action

examples.target: She does speak Russian, you know.
Do come in and sit down.
examples.en: emphatic do in a polite imperative

rules.title: Negative and time clefts: It is not that ..., It was not until ...
rules.body: 'It is not that ... (it is that ...)' corrects a likely misreading of motives: 'It's not that I dislike him; it's that I distrust him.' 'It was not until ... that' and 'It is only when ... that' focus a time condition and are the ordinary equivalents of the inverted forms in chapter 1. Both halves must be complete: the that-clause cannot be dropped in writing.

examples.target: It is not that I dislike him; it is that I distrust him.
It was not until the following morning that the error was discovered.
It is only when the fog lifts that we can see the coast.

rules.title: Shell nouns as emphatic frames: The trouble is, the question is
rules.body: Nouns such as trouble, problem, point, fact, question and truth can open a sentence and present the main message as their complement: 'The trouble is that nobody checked'; 'The question is whether the budget will stretch.' In speech the 'that' is often dropped and the frame works like a cleft, pushing the key information to the end. In formal writing keep 'that' and avoid the redundant 'is, is'.

examples.target: The trouble is that nobody read the manual.
The question is whether we can afford it.
The fact is that we were simply outplayed.

rules.title: Agreement and pronoun case in clefts
rules.body: In an it-cleft the verb of the that-clause agrees with the focused noun: 'It is the children who are tired'; with a first-person pronoun, formal English uses the subject form and matching verb: 'It is I who am responsible', while informal English prefers 'It's me who is'. In wh-clefts, 'be' is singular unless the complement is plural: 'What matters is the detail' but 'What matter are the details' is possible, and 'What I need are two volunteers' is widely accepted.

examples.target: It is I who am responsible.
examples.en: formal: subject pronoun and matching verb

examples.target: It is the children who are tired.
examples.en: verb agrees with the focused noun

examples.target: What I need are two more volunteers.
examples.en: plural verb with a plural complement

exercises.q: Which element is emphasised in 'It was Tom who broke the vase'?
exercises.explain: The element placed after 'it was' is the focus of an it-cleft.

exercises.q: ___ I really need is a quiet weekend. (wh-word)
exercises.explain: A wh-cleft begins with a what-clause acting as subject.

exercises.q: A cleft sentence can focus the main verb directly, as in 'It was broke that he the vase.'
exercises.explain: An it-cleft can focus any element except the verb itself.

exercises.q: Rewrite as an it-cleft focusing 'in Lisbon': 'We met in Lisbon.' → It was in Lisbon ___ we met. (one word)
exercises.explain: 'That' is the default link after the focused element.

pairs: It was the dog that ate it.

exercises.answer: What annoys me most is his constant lateness.
exercises.en: His constant lateness annoys me most (wh-cleft).

exercises.q: All I want ___ a cup of tea.
exercises.explain: The all-clause is a singular subject and takes 'is'.

exercises.q: Rewrite with emphatic do: 'I warned you.' → I ___ warn you. (one word)
exercises.explain: Past emphatic 'did' carries the tense; the main verb returns to the base form.

exercises.q: 'It was not until midnight that the votes were counted' is a correct cleft of a time expression.
exercises.explain: 'It was not until ... that' is the standard negative time cleft.

exercises.q: The reason ___ the launch was postponed was that the tests failed.
exercises.explain: 'The reason why ... was that' is the formal pattern; 'because' would be redundant.

exercises.q: What she did next ___ surprise everyone. (one word; a bare infinitive follows)
exercises.explain: In a do-cleft, 'be' links the what-clause to a bare infinitive.

exercises.answer: It was the manager, not the staff, who made the decision.
exercises.en: The manager, not the staff, made the decision (contrastive it-cleft).

exercises.q: Which sentence uses the wh-cleft correctly?
options: What happened was that the server crashed.
What happened was the server crashed it.
What was happened that the server crashed.
What the server crashed was happened.
exercises.explain: 'What happened was that ...' focuses the whole event in a that-clause.

exercises.q: In formal writing, 'The reason is because ...' is widely regarded as redundant, and 'The reason is that ...' is preferred.
exercises.explain: 'Reason' already expresses cause, so editors prefer 'that'.

exercises.q: Rewrite focusing the time: 'We moved here in 2010.' → It ___ in 2010 that we moved here. (one word)
exercises.explain: The tense of 'be' in the cleft matches the past tense of the clause.

pairs: singles out one element for contrast
emphasises the action as a whole
shell noun introducing the main point

exercises.q: It is I ___ responsible. (formal)
exercises.explain: Formal usage keeps the subject pronoun 'I' and the verb agrees with it.

exercises.q: It ___ the quality that put me off but the price. (negative past form of 'be')
exercises.explain: A negative it-cleft contrasts the rejected focus with the real one.

exercises.answer: It was not until the following morning that the error was discovered.
exercises.en: The error was discovered only the following morning.

exercises.q: 'What I need are two more volunteers' is acceptable: with a plural complement the verb may be plural.
exercises.explain: Plural agreement with a plural complement is widely accepted in wh-clefts.

exercises.q: Spot the error.
options: What she said it was true.
It was in May that we met.
exercises.explain: The what-clause is already the subject; the extra pronoun 'it' is ungrammatical.

exercises.q: Rewrite as a reversed wh-cleft: 'What we lack is time.' → Time is ___ we lack. (one word)
exercises.explain: In the reversed cleft the what-clause follows 'be'.

exercises.q: The question ___ whether the budget will stretch.
exercises.explain: A shell noun like 'question' takes 'is' + a whether-clause directly.

exercises.q: It is not that I dislike him; it is ___ I distrust him. (one word)
exercises.explain: 'It is not that ..., it is that ...' corrects a presumed motive.

exercises.answer: The reason why she left was never explained.
exercises.en: Nobody ever explained why she left.

exercises.q: In 'She does speak Russian', 'does' adds emphasis and is stressed in speech.
exercises.explain: Emphatic 'do' is always stressed and contradicts or confirms an assumption.

pairs: It was only when the fog lifted
The place where we first met

exercises.q: Rewrite with 'The thing': 'Her honesty impresses me most.' → The thing ___ impresses me most is her honesty. (relative pronoun)
exercises.explain: 'The thing that/which ... is' is the informal counterpart of a what-cleft.

exercises.q: Which is the most natural way to emphasise 'yesterday' in 'I saw him yesterday'?
options: It was yesterday that I saw him.
Yesterday was when I saw him it.
It was yesterday when I saw him it.
What I saw him was yesterday.
exercises.explain: An it-cleft with 'that' focuses the time adverbial cleanly.

exercises.answer: What the committee failed to consider was the cost.
exercises.en: The committee failed to consider the cost (wh-cleft).

sections.title: Conditionals beyond the basics
sections.summary: Beyond the three textbook conditionals, proficient English mixes time frames, inverts the if-clause, uses 'were to' and 'should' for tentativeness, and replaces 'if' with 'but for', 'provided that', 'unless' and implied conditions. This chapter maps those forms and the errors that typically betray a non-native writer.

rules.title: Mixed conditionals
rules.body: The two halves of a conditional need not share a time frame. A past unreal condition can have a present result: 'If I had taken the job, I would be living in Paris now' (past perfect + would + infinitive). A present or permanent condition can have a past result: 'If she weren't so stubborn, she would have apologised' (past simple + would have + past participle). The time adverbs (now, yesterday, still) usually make the mix explicit.

examples.target: If I had taken the job, I would be living in Paris now.
If she weren't so stubborn, she would have apologised.
If we had saved more, we wouldn't be in debt today.
examples.en: past condition, present result with today

rules.title: Inverted conditionals: had, were, should
rules.body: In formal style 'if' can be dropped and the auxiliary fronted. Third conditional: 'Had I known, I would have called.' Second with 'be': 'Were she here, she would object.' First, tentative: 'Should you need anything, ring reception.' Only these three auxiliaries invert; negatives are not contracted: 'Had it not been for the delay ...', never *Hadn't it been. The structure is common in business letters, contracts and journalism.

examples.target: Had the alarm sounded earlier, nobody would have been hurt.
Were it not for the rain, we would be outside.
Should the payment not arrive, the order will be cancelled.

rules.title: Were to and should for remoteness and tentativeness
rules.body: 'If + subject + were to + infinitive' presents a future possibility as remote or hypothetical: 'If you were to lose your passport, contact the embassy.' It can be inverted: 'Were he to resign, the party would collapse.' 'If + subject + should' (or inverted 'Should you ...') presents a real possibility politely or tentatively, often in instructions: 'If you should see Dan, tell him.' 'Happen to' adds the same tentativeness: 'If you happen to see Dan ...'.

examples.target: If the bridge were to collapse, the town would be cut off.
examples.en: were to for a remote hypothesis

examples.target: Were he to resign, the party would collapse.
If you should see Dan, tell him I called.
examples.en: should for a tentative real possibility

examples.target: If you happen to pass a chemist's, buy some aspirin.
examples.en: happen to with the same effect

rules.title: But for, without, if it weren't for, had it not been for
rules.body: 'But for' + noun phrase means 'if it were not for / if it had not been for' and is formal: 'But for your help, I would have failed.' 'Without' works similarly in neutral style. The full forms are 'if it weren't for' (present or general) and 'if it hadn't been for' (past), with inverted equivalents 'were it not for' and 'had it not been for'. The result clause takes the usual would / would have.

examples.target: But for the goalkeeper, we would have lost the match.
examples.en: but for + noun = if it had not been for

examples.target: If it weren't for the noise, this flat would be perfect.
examples.en: present unreal: if it weren't for

examples.target: Had it not been for the delay, we'd have caught the train.

rules.title: Unless, provided that, as long as, in case and other conjunctions
rules.body: 'Unless' means 'except if' and is already negative, so *unless you don't is wrong. It is awkward with unreal past results: 'If he hadn't helped, I'd have failed' cannot become *Unless he had helped. 'Provided (that)', 'providing (that)', 'as long as', 'so long as' and 'on condition that' set a requirement: 'Provided that you pay in advance, delivery is free.' 'In case' expresses a precaution, not a condition: 'Take an umbrella in case it rains' (because it may rain). 'Supposing', 'suppose' and 'assuming (that)' introduce hypotheses.

examples.target: Unless you pay today, you will be fined.
examples.en: unless = except if, no second negative

examples.target: Provided that the weather holds, we sail on Monday.
Take an umbrella in case it rains.
Suppose we missed the flight; what then?

rules.title: Will and would inside the if-clause
rules.body: The rule that 'will' never follows 'if' has exceptions. 'If you will' expresses willingness or a polite request: 'If you will wait a moment, I'll check.' Stressed 'will' expresses insistence: 'If you will keep interrupting, we'll never finish.' 'Will' also appears when the if-clause states a result that motivates the main clause: 'If it will help, I'll come.' 'Would' makes requests more polite: 'If you would sign here, we can proceed.'

examples.target: If you will wait a moment, I'll check.
If you will keep interrupting, we'll never finish.
If it will help, I'll come with you.
examples.en: will for a result that motivates

examples.target: If you would sign here, we can proceed.

rules.title: Were, as if and the subjunctive after if
rules.body: In unreal conditions 'were' is used for all persons in formal English: 'If I were you'; 'If he were here'. 'Was' is accepted in informal speech but not in formal writing, and never in the inverted form (*Was I you). 'As if' and 'as though' take the same unreal past or past perfect: 'She behaved as if nothing had happened'; 'He talks as though he were the boss.' Other tenses are possible in the if-clause when the meaning calls for them: 'If you've finished, we can go'; 'If she was driving, she wasn't drinking.'

examples.target: Were I you, I would wait.
She behaved as if nothing had happened.
examples.en: as if + past perfect for an unreal past

examples.target: If you've finished, we can go.
examples.en: present perfect in a real condition

rules.title: Implied conditionals
rules.body: Conditions are often implied rather than stated with 'if'. 'Otherwise' and 'or else' mean 'if not': 'Hurry up; otherwise we'll miss the train.' 'With' and 'without' + noun phrase: 'Without the subsidy, the farm would fold.' A to-infinitive: 'To hear him talk, you'd think he owned the place.' 'Failing that', 'in that case', 'given + noun' and 'in the event of' are formal connectors with conditional force. The verb forms in the main clause follow the usual conditional logic.

examples.target: Hurry up; otherwise we'll miss the train.
To hear him talk, you'd think he owned the place.
examples.en: infinitive implying if you heard him

examples.target: Failing that, try the branch office.
examples.en: failing that = if that does not work

rules.title: Wishes, preferences and even if
rules.body: 'If only' and 'wish' use the past for present wishes, the past perfect for regrets and 'would' for annoyance about someone else's behaviour: 'If only I had listened!'; 'I wish he would stop.' 'Would rather' + subject takes a past form for a present wish: 'I'd rather you didn't smoke in here.' 'Even if' introduces a condition that makes no difference ('Even if it rains, we'll go'), whereas 'even though' states a fact. 'Whether or not' covers both alternatives: 'Whether or not you agree, it will happen.'

examples.target: If only I had listened to her advice!
examples.en: if only + past perfect for regret

examples.target: I'd rather you didn't smoke in here.
Even if it rains, we'll go.
examples.en: even if: condition that makes no difference

exercises.q: If I ___ the job, I would be living in Paris now.
exercises.explain: A past unreal condition (past perfect) with a present result is a mixed conditional.

exercises.q: Rewrite without 'if': 'If I had known, I would have called.' → ___ I known, I would have called.
exercises.explain: The auxiliary 'had' is fronted and 'if' is dropped.

exercises.q: 'Hadn't I known' is the correct negative of 'Had I known'.
exercises.explain: Inverted conditionals do not contract: 'Had I not known'.

exercises.q: ___ your help, I would never have finished.
exercises.explain: 'But for' + noun means 'if it had not been for'.

exercises.answer: Were it not for the rain, we would be outside.
exercises.en: If it weren't for the rain, we would be outside.

exercises.q: If you ___ to lose your passport, contact the embassy at once. (tentative form of 'be')
exercises.explain: 'Were to' presents the possibility as remote.

exercises.q: Which sentence is a mixed conditional?
options: If she had studied, she would have passed.
If she had studied medicine, she would be a doctor now.
If she studied, she would pass.
If she studies, she will pass.
exercises.explain: A past perfect condition is combined with a present result ('would be ... now').

exercises.q: 'Should you need anything, call reception' means the same as 'If you should need anything, call reception'.
exercises.explain: Inverted 'should' is simply the formal, if-less version.

exercises.q: Rewrite with inversion: 'If he were to resign, the party would collapse.' → ___ he to resign, the party would collapse.
exercises.explain: 'Were' is fronted and 'if' is dropped; 'to resign' stays.

exercises.q: If you ___ keep interrupting, we'll never finish. (insistence)
exercises.explain: Stressed 'will' in an if-clause expresses stubborn insistence.

exercises.answer: Had the alarm sounded earlier, nobody would have been hurt.
exercises.en: If the alarm had sounded earlier, nobody would have been hurt.

exercises.q: Take an umbrella ___ it rains. (precaution, two words)
exercises.explain: 'In case' expresses a precaution, not a condition.

exercises.q: 'Unless he had helped me, I would have failed' is a natural equivalent of 'If he hadn't helped me, I would have failed'.
exercises.explain: 'Unless' is awkward with unreal past results; use 'if ... not' or 'but for his help'.

exercises.q: I'd have accepted, ___ the salary.
exercises.explain: A past unreal result needs the past form 'if it hadn't been for'.

exercises.q: If only I ___ listened to her advice! (regret about the past, one word)
exercises.explain: 'If only' + past perfect expresses regret about the past.

pairs: To hear him talk, you'd think he owned the place.
Without the subsidy, the farm would fold.
Failing that, try the branch office.

exercises.answer: Should the payment not arrive, the order will be cancelled.
exercises.en: If the payment doesn't arrive, the order will be cancelled.

exercises.q: If it ___ help, I'll come with you.
exercises.explain: 'Will' is used in an if-clause when the clause states a result that motivates the offer.

exercises.q: Rewrite with inversion: 'If you should change your mind, let me know.' → ___ you change your mind, let me know.
exercises.explain: 'Should' is fronted and 'if' is dropped.

exercises.q: In 'If she weren't so stubborn, she would have apologised', a present state is linked to a past result.
exercises.explain: Past simple condition (present state) + would have (past result) is a mixed conditional.

exercises.q: Which is correct?
options: Were I you, I would wait.
Was I you, I would wait.
If I would be you, I would wait.
Were I be you, I would wait.
exercises.explain: Only 'were' can be inverted; 'was' and 'would' are not possible here.

exercises.q: She behaved as ___ nothing had happened. (one word)
exercises.explain: 'As if / as though' + past perfect describes an unreal past.

exercises.answer: But for the goalkeeper, we would have lost the match.
exercises.en: If it hadn't been for the goalkeeper, we would have lost.

exercises.q: Choose the formal equivalent of 'If you happen to see Dan, tell him.'
options: Should you see Dan, tell him.
Had you seen Dan, tell him.
Were you seen Dan, tell him.
Unless you see Dan, tell him.
exercises.explain: Inverted 'should' carries the same tentative, real-possibility meaning.

exercises.q: 'Provided that' and 'providing that' are both acceptable; the former is slightly more formal.
exercises.explain: Both set a condition; 'provided that' is the commoner choice in formal texts.

exercises.q: Rewrite: 'If it hadn't been for the delay, we'd have caught the train.' → ___ it not been for the delay, we'd have caught the train.
exercises.explain: Inverted form with uncontracted 'not' after the subject.

exercises.q: Spot the error.
options: If you would sign here, we can proceed.
Had I been informed, I would have objected.
Unless you don't pay, you will be fined.
Suppose we missed the flight, what then?
exercises.explain: 'Unless' is already negative; the sentence should read 'Unless you pay'.

exercises.answer: If the bridge were to collapse, the town would be cut off.
exercises.en: In the remote event of the bridge collapsing, the town would be cut off.

exercises.q: I'd rather you ___ smoke in here. (past form for a present wish)
exercises.explain: 'Would rather' + subject takes a past form for a present preference.

pairs: If I had saved, I would be rich now.
Had we left earlier, we would have arrived.
If it were to snow, the match would be off.

sections.title: Participle and reduced clauses
sections.summary: Participle clauses compress a subordinate clause into a phrase: 'Having finished the report, she left.' This chapter covers present, past and perfect participles, absolute clauses with their own subject, reduced relative clauses and the dangling participle, the error that most reliably marks careless writing.

rules.title: Present participle clauses
rules.body: An -ing clause with the same subject as the main clause can express time, reason or an accompanying action: 'Walking home, I noticed the lights were off' (= As I walked home). The relationship is left implicit, so the reader infers it from context. The clause usually comes first, set off by a comma, but can follow the main clause: 'She left early, saying she felt ill.'

examples.target: Walking home, I noticed the lights were off.
Not knowing the area, we asked a local for directions.
examples.en: reason: because we did not know

examples.target: She left early, saying she felt ill.
examples.en: accompanying action after the main clause

rules.title: Perfect participle: having + past participle
rules.body: 'Having' + past participle shows that the action of the participle clause was completed before that of the main clause: 'Having finished the report, she left.' The simple -ing form implies simultaneity or close sequence ('Opening the door, she saw ...'), so 'having' is needed when the gap in time matters or when the sequence would otherwise be unclear. The passive is 'having been' + past participle.

examples.target: Having finished the report, she went home.
Having locked the door, she realised her keys were inside.
Having been warned twice, he still ignored the advice.

rules.title: Past participle clauses
rules.body: A past participle clause has passive meaning and shares the subject of the main clause: 'Built in 1850, the mill still runs' (= which was built). It can express time, reason or condition: 'Seen from above, the city looks tiny'; 'Exhausted by the climb, the runners collapsed.' Adjectives behave the same way: 'Unable to sleep, he got up.'

examples.target: Built in 1850, the mill still runs.
Seen from above, the city looks tiny.
Exhausted, the runners collapsed at the finish.

rules.title: Dangling participles
rules.body: The implied subject of a participle clause must be the subject of the main clause. *'Walking down the street, the trees looked beautiful' makes the trees walk. Correct it by giving the participle its proper subject ('As I walked down the street, the trees ...') or by changing the main clause subject ('Walking down the street, I admired the trees'). A few fixed expressions are exempt because they refer to the speaker: generally speaking, considering, judging by, given, provided, taking everything into account.

examples.target: Walking down the street, I admired the trees.
As I was driving to work, a deer ran across the road.
Generally speaking, the results are encouraging.

rules.title: Absolute clauses: a participle with its own subject
rules.body: When the participle has a different subject, that subject is stated inside the clause, making an absolute clause: 'The rain having stopped, we set off'; 'The roads being icy, the race was cancelled.' 'With' + noun + participle is a commoner, slightly less formal version: 'With the deadline approaching, the team worked all night.' Fixed absolutes include 'weather permitting', 'all things considered', 'that said' and 'present company excepted'.

examples.target: The rain having stopped, we set off.
examples.en: absolute clause with its own subject

examples.target: With the deadline approaching, the team worked through the night.
Weather permitting, we sail at six.
All things considered, it was a successful launch.
examples.en: fixed absolute with a past participle

rules.title: Reduced relative clauses
rules.body: A relative clause whose pronoun is the subject can be reduced: active clauses to an -ing form ('the man who is standing by the door' → 'the man standing by the door'), passive ones to a past participle ('the documents that were sent' → 'the documents sent'), and 'be' + adjective to the adjective alone ('the people who are responsible' → 'the people responsible'). After ordinals, superlatives, 'next', 'last' and 'only', a to-infinitive is used: 'the first woman to reach the summit'. A clause whose pronoun is the object cannot be reduced: *'the book I reading'.

examples.target: The man standing by the door is my uncle.
The documents sent yesterday have arrived.
She was the first woman to reach the summit.
The staff available today are all new.

rules.title: Participles after conjunctions and prepositions
rules.body: Participles can follow 'when', 'while', 'if', 'unless', 'although', 'though', 'once', 'until', 'before', 'after' and prepositions such as 'on', 'despite', 'instead of', 'without': 'when asked', 'if necessary', 'while waiting', 'on hearing the news', 'despite being tired'. The understood subject is still the main-clause subject. This pattern is compact and common in formal and technical prose.

examples.target: When asked about the merger, she declined to comment.
On hearing the news, she burst into tears.
Although exhausted, he kept going.

rules.title: Negative forms and participles of result
rules.body: 'Not' or 'never' goes before the participle: 'Not wanting to wake her, I tiptoed out'; 'Never having seen snow, the children were speechless'; 'Not having been informed, the director was annoyed.' A participle clause placed after the main clause often expresses result: 'The storm hit at dawn, leaving thousands without power'; 'thereby' or 'thus' can make this explicit: 'The company cut prices, thereby forcing its rivals to follow.'

examples.target: Not wanting to wake her, I tiptoed out.
Never having seen snow, the children were speechless.
The storm hit the coast at dawn, leaving thousands without power.
The company cut prices, thereby forcing its rivals to follow.

rules.title: Register, punctuation and overuse
rules.body: Participle clauses are a mark of written, formal English; in speech full clauses are more natural. A fronted participle clause is followed by a comma, and a non-defining one after the main clause is preceded by one; reduced relatives inside the noun phrase take no commas. Chains of participle clauses become hard to follow, and 'being' + adjective for reason ('Being tired, I left') can sound stiff; prefer a full clause when the logical link is important.

examples.target: Anyone wishing to attend should register by Friday.
Being a foreigner, I found the customs strange.
examples.en: being-clause of reason with a matching subject

examples.target: The meeting having ended early, everyone went for lunch.
examples.en: absolute clause, comma before the main clause

exercises.q: ___ finished the report, she went home.
exercises.explain: The perfect participle shows the report was finished before she left.

exercises.q: 'Walking down the street, the trees looked beautiful' is correctly formed.
exercises.explain: The participle dangles: the trees are not walking.

exercises.q: Reduce the relative clause: 'The man who is standing by the door is my uncle.' → The man ___ by the door is my uncle. (one word)
exercises.explain: A subject relative with an active verb reduces to the -ing form.

pairs: Having read the letter, he wept.
Built in 1850, the mill still runs.
The rain having stopped, we left.
absolute clause with its own subject
Weather permitting, we sail at six.

exercises.answer: Not knowing the area, we asked a local for directions.
exercises.en: Because we didn't know the area, we asked a local.

exercises.q: Which sentence contains a dangling participle?
options: Having lost the key, I called a locksmith.
Being late, the bus was missed by me.
Seen from above, the city looks tiny.
exercises.explain: The bus was not late; the implied subject of 'being late' is the speaker.

exercises.q: Reduce: 'The documents that were sent yesterday have arrived.' → The documents ___ yesterday have arrived.
exercises.explain: A passive subject relative reduces to the past participle.

exercises.q: 'Generally speaking' is an accepted fixed expression even though its subject does not match the main clause.
exercises.explain: A handful of speaker-oriented phrases are exempt from the dangling rule.

exercises.q: She was the first woman ___ the summit.
exercises.explain: After an ordinal, the reduced relative takes a to-infinitive.

exercises.q: ___ been warned twice, he still ignored the advice. (one word)
exercises.explain: 'Having been' + past participle is the perfect passive participle.

exercises.answer: With the deadline approaching, the team worked through the night.
exercises.en: As the deadline approached, the team worked all night.

exercises.q: Rewrite 'Because I didn't want to wake her, I tiptoed out' with a participle clause.
options: Not wanting to wake her, I tiptoed out.
Wanting not to wake her, I tiptoed out.
Not to wanting wake her, I tiptoed out.
No wanting to wake her, I tiptoed out.
exercises.explain: 'Not' goes directly before the participle.

exercises.q: The storm hit the coast at dawn, ___ thousands without power. (participle of 'leave')
exercises.explain: An -ing clause after the main clause expresses result.

exercises.q: A relative clause can be reduced to a participle only when the relative pronoun is the subject of its clause.
exercises.explain: Object relatives like 'the book I am reading' cannot be reduced.

pairs: when he or she was asked
while he or she was waiting
although he or she was exhausted

exercises.q: Spot the error.
options: Having been delayed, the flight landed at noon.
The people responsible have been identified.
Looking out of the window, a car was parked outside.
Taken as a whole, the results are encouraging.
exercises.explain: The car was not looking out of the window: the participle dangles.

exercises.q: Rewrite: 'After she had locked the door, she realised her keys were inside.' → ___ locked the door, she realised her keys were inside. (one word)
exercises.explain: The perfect participle replaces 'after she had'.

exercises.answer: The meeting having ended early, everyone went for lunch.
exercises.en: Because the meeting ended early, everyone went for lunch.

exercises.q: All things ___, it was a successful launch.
exercises.explain: 'All things considered' is a fixed absolute with a passive past participle.

exercises.q: Never ___ seen snow, the children were speechless. (one word)
exercises.explain: 'Never having' + past participle is the negative perfect participle.

exercises.q: 'Being a foreigner, the customs were strange to me' is correctly formed.
exercises.explain: The main-clause subject is 'the customs', which are not the foreigner.

exercises.answer: Anyone wishing to attend should register by Friday.
exercises.en: Anyone who wishes to attend should register by Friday.

exercises.q: The company cut prices, ___ forcing its rivals to follow.
exercises.explain: 'Thereby' + -ing makes the result relationship explicit.

exercises.q: Reduce: 'Those who were injured in the crash were taken to hospital.' → Those ___ in the crash were taken to hospital.
exercises.explain: Passive subject relative → past participle.

pairs: the only candidate who survived the first round
the only candidate to survive the first round
the car which is parked outside
the students who are taking the exam
the staff who are available today

exercises.q: In 'Having finished the report, she left', the finishing clearly came before the leaving.
exercises.explain: The perfect participle marks the earlier action.

exercises.q: Rewrite with an absolute clause: 'Because the roads were icy, the race was cancelled.' → The roads ___ icy, the race was cancelled. (one word)
exercises.explain: The absolute clause keeps its own subject and uses 'being'.

exercises.answer: Not having been informed, the director was understandably annoyed.
exercises.en: Because he had not been informed, the director was annoyed.

exercises.q: Which is the best correction of 'Driving to work, a deer ran across the road'?
options: As I was driving to work, a deer ran across the road.
Driving to work, a deer was run across the road.
A deer ran across the road, driving to work.
Driving to work, the road had a deer on it.
exercises.explain: A full clause restores the real subject of the driving.

exercises.q: On ___ the news, she burst into tears. (participle of 'hear')
exercises.explain: 'On' + -ing means 'as soon as'.

sections.title: The subjunctive and formal mood
sections.summary: The English subjunctive survives in a few well-defined places: after verbs of demand and recommendation ('insist that he be'), in unreal 'were', in fixed formulas such as 'God forbid' and 'be that as it may', and after 'lest'. This chapter sets out where it is required, where 'should' can replace it, and how the choice between subjunctive and indicative changes meaning.

rules.title: The mandative subjunctive after verbs of demand and suggestion
rules.body: After verbs such as insist, demand, recommend, suggest, propose, request, require, ask, urge and order, the that-clause takes the base form of the verb for every person: 'The committee insisted that the report be published'; 'She recommended that he attend.' The negative is 'that he not be'; the passive is 'that it be done'. American English uses this form almost exclusively; British English also allows 'should' + base ('insisted that he should be') and, informally, the plain indicative ('insisted that he is'), which formal writing avoids.

examples.target: The judge ordered that the prisoner be released immediately.
examples.en: base form be after ordered that

examples.target: She asked that he not be disturbed.
examples.en: negative subjunctive: not before the verb

examples.target: We propose that the fee should be waived.
The rules require that each member attend.

rules.title: Adjective and noun triggers
rules.body: The same subjunctive follows adjectives of necessity or desirability in 'it is ... that': essential, vital, imperative, important, crucial, necessary, desirable, advisable: 'It is vital that the samples be kept cold.' It also follows nouns derived from the trigger verbs: 'the requirement that every visitor wear a badge', 'his suggestion that we leave', 'a proposal that the meeting be adjourned'.

examples.target: It is essential that every visitor wear a badge.
examples.en: it is essential that + base form

examples.target: It is imperative that she be told at once.
The proposal that the meeting be adjourned was accepted.

rules.title: The were-subjunctive
rules.body: 'Were' replaces 'was' in unreal conditions and comparisons for all persons: 'If I were you'; 'Were I in charge'; 'as if it were'; 'I wish it were Friday'; 'I'd rather it were otherwise'; 'Suppose he were to refuse.' 'Was' is heard in informal speech ('If I was you') but is marked in formal writing, and inversion requires 'were'. Note that 'if ... was' is correct when the condition is real and past: 'If she was there, she saw it.'

examples.target: I wish it were Friday already.
examples.en: wish + were for a present wish

examples.target: He treats the office as though it were his private club.
Were I in charge, things would change.

rules.title: Formulaic subjunctives
rules.body: A set of fixed expressions preserves the old subjunctive: 'God forbid', 'God save the King', 'Long live the Republic', 'so be it', 'be that as it may', 'far be it from me to ...', 'suffice it to say', 'come what may', 'heaven help us', 'if need be', 'as it were', 'perish the thought', 'be it ... or ...'. They are not productive: the verb is fixed and cannot be changed for person or tense. Most are formal or literary, though 'if need be' and 'so be it' are common in speech.

examples.target: Be that as it may, the decision has been taken.
Far be it from me to criticise, but the figures do not add up.
Suffice it to say that the talks did not go well.
If need be, we can postpone the launch.

rules.title: Lest, for fear that and whether ... be
rules.body: 'Lest' means 'for fear that' or 'in order that ... not' and is followed by the base form or 'should': 'She spoke softly lest the baby wake'; 'Keep the receipt lest you should need it.' It is formal and slightly archaic but still used in careful writing. 'Whether it be ... or ...' is a concessive subjunctive meaning 'no matter whether': 'Whether it be rain or shine, the parade goes ahead.' The formal 'however ... may be' and 'whatever the cost may be' belong to the same register.

examples.target: She spoke softly, lest the baby wake up.
He wrote it down lest he should forget.
Whether it be rain or shine, the parade goes ahead.

rules.title: Putative and emotive should
rules.body: Beyond its use as a subjunctive substitute, 'should' appears in that-clauses after expressions of surprise, regret or judgement, where it conveys the speaker's attitude rather than obligation: 'It is odd that he should have left without a word'; 'I'm sorry that it should have come to this.' In rhetorical questions it expresses indignation: 'Why should I apologise?' It is also used after 'in case' and 'for fear that' in formal style: 'in case anyone should ask'.

examples.target: It is odd that he should have left without a word.
examples.en: emotive should after it is odd that

examples.target: Why should I apologise when I did nothing wrong?
Take a key in case anyone should arrive early.

rules.title: Wishes, preferences and 'it's time'
rules.body: 'Wish' and 'if only' take the past simple for present wishes, the past perfect for regrets, and 'would' for irritation at others' behaviour: 'I wish you would listen.' 'It's (high/about) time' + subject takes the past simple with present meaning: 'It's time we went home.' 'Would rather' and 'would sooner' + subject do the same: 'I'd rather you stayed.' The literary 'would that ...' expresses a wish: 'Would that it were true!'

examples.target: It's time we went home; it's nearly midnight.
I'd rather you stayed until the end.
Would that it were true!

rules.title: Optative and official formulas
rules.body: Wishes and blessings use 'may' + subject + base form: 'May the best team win'; 'May you both be happy'; 'Long may it continue.' Official and legal texts open with inverted 'be it': 'Be it resolved that ...', 'Be it enacted ...', and use 'let it be known'. Diplomatic distancing uses 'would' and the past: 'I would suggest', 'I was wondering whether you might ...'. These are rhetorical registers; using them in ordinary conversation sounds ironic.

examples.target: May the best team win.
Be it resolved that the motion is carried.
I would suggest that we wait a week.

rules.title: Subjunctive versus indicative: a change of meaning
rules.body: With verbs like insist, suggest and demand, mood changes meaning. 'They insisted that he was innocent' reports an assertion of fact; 'They insisted that he be released' makes a demand. 'She suggested that he was lying' = she implied it; 'She suggested that he leave' = she advised it. Avoid *'suggest him to go' and *'suggest that he will go'; use the subjunctive, 'should', or a gerund ('suggest going').

examples.target: They insisted that he was innocent.
They insisted that he be released.
I suggest that he go. / I suggest going.
examples.en: correct alternatives to suggest him to go

exercises.q: The committee insisted that the report ___ published in full.
exercises.explain: After 'insisted that' expressing a demand, the clause takes the base form 'be'.

exercises.q: It is essential that every visitor ___ a badge. (base form of 'wear')
exercises.explain: The mandative subjunctive has no third-person -s.

exercises.q: 'If I was you, I'd accept' is acceptable in informal speech, but 'were' is expected in formal writing.
exercises.explain: The were-subjunctive is the formal standard for unreal conditions.

exercises.answer: The judge ordered that the prisoner be released immediately.
exercises.en: The judge demanded the prisoner's immediate release.

exercises.q: Which negative is correct in the mandative subjunctive?
options: She asked that he not be disturbed.
She asked that he not been disturbed.
She asked that he doesn't be disturbed.
She asked that he isn't disturbed.
exercises.explain: 'Not' precedes the base form; no 'do' is used.

exercises.q: I wish it ___ Friday already. (subjunctive of 'be')
exercises.explain: 'Wish' + were expresses a present unreal wish.

exercises.q: 'They insisted that he was innocent' means the same as 'They insisted that he be innocent'.
exercises.explain: The indicative asserts a fact; the subjunctive expresses a demand.

exercises.q: Keep the receipt ___ you need to return it. (formal: 'for fear that')
exercises.explain: 'Lest' means 'for fear that' and takes the base form.

exercises.q: She spoke softly, lest the baby ___ up. (base form of 'wake', or should + base)
exercises.explain: 'Lest' is followed by the base form or 'should' + base.

exercises.answer: It is vital that the samples be kept at a constant temperature.
exercises.en: The samples must be kept at a constant temperature.

exercises.q: Rewrite in British style with 'should': 'We propose that the fee be waived.'
options: We propose that the fee should be waived.
We propose that the fee should waive.
We propose the fee should to be waived.
We propose that should the fee be waived.
exercises.explain: 'Should' + base form replaces the bare subjunctive.

exercises.q: Long ___ the Queen! (formulaic subjunctive of 'live')
exercises.explain: Fixed optative formula with the base form.

exercises.q: In 'It is odd that he should have left without a word', 'should' expresses obligation.
exercises.explain: This is emotive (putative) 'should', conveying the speaker's surprise.

exercises.q: He treats the office as though it ___ his private club. (formal unreal comparison)
exercises.explain: 'As though' + were marks the comparison as unreal in formal style.

sections.title: Nominalisation, hedging and academic register
sections.summary: Academic and professional English packs actions into nouns ('the implementation of the policy'), softens claims with hedges ('appears to', 'tends to', 'it is arguable that') and prefers impersonal, Latinate wording. This chapter shows how to build and unpack nominalisations, how to calibrate caution with verbs, modals and adverbs, and how to avoid both over- and under-hedging.

rules.title: Building nominalisations
rules.body: A verb or adjective can be turned into a noun so that an action or quality becomes a thing to be discussed: implement → implementation, fail → failure, resist → resistance, emerge → emergence, accurate → accuracy. 'They implemented the policy quickly' becomes 'The rapid implementation of the policy'. The subject and object of the verb typically reappear as possessives or of-phrases: 'the company's expansion', 'the acquisition of the firm'.

examples.target: The rapid implementation of the policy met resistance.
The company's rapid expansion worried investors.
The construction of the bridge took three years.

rules.title: Why nominalise, and when to unpack
rules.body: Nominalisation lets a writer put a whole proposition in subject position, link it to a previous sentence ('This failure ...') and keep a formal, impersonal tone. Overused, it produces abstract, agentless prose: 'The utilisation of the facility by staff showed an increase' hides a simple fact, 'Staff used the facility more.' Unpack when the agent matters, when the sentence has stacked more than two abstract nouns, or when a verb would be clearer.

examples.target: Staff used the facility more.
A decision was taken to close the plant.
examples.en: nominalisation plus passive hides who decided

examples.target: The failure of the talks was widely attributed to mistrust.

rules.title: Hedging verbs: appear, seem, tend, suggest, indicate
rules.body: Hedging verbs present a claim as an interpretation rather than a fact. 'Appear to' and 'seem to' signal that the evidence points one way; 'tend to' states a general pattern with exceptions; 'suggest', 'indicate' and 'point to' are the standard verbs for reporting what data show. 'Prove', 'demonstrate' and 'establish' are strong and should be reserved for conclusive evidence.

examples.target: The data appear to suggest a seasonal effect.
Smaller firms tend to adopt the technology later.
examples.en: tend to for a general pattern

examples.target: The results suggest a link between the two variables.

rules.title: Modal hedging: may, might, could, would
rules.body: 'May' and 'might' mark a claim as possible; 'could' adds a sense of hypothesis; 'would' in 'it would appear' or 'it would seem' makes an inference deliberately tentative. 'May well' strengthens a possibility without asserting it. Use one modal hedge per claim; piling them up ('it might perhaps possibly be the case that') weakens the writing rather than the claim.

examples.target: This may explain the discrepancy.
It would appear that the sample was contaminated.
Costs may well rise next year.

rules.title: Impersonal frames: it is arguable that, it could be argued that
rules.body: Academic writing often attributes a claim to no one in particular: 'It is arguable that ...', 'It could be argued that ...', 'It is widely held that ...', 'It is generally accepted that ...', 'There is evidence that ...', 'It would seem that ...'. These frames let the writer present a position without owning it fully and are especially useful when introducing a view that will later be qualified or rejected.

examples.target: It is arguable that the reforms were introduced too late.
examples.en: it is arguable that = one could argue

examples.target: It could be argued that the policy has failed.
It is generally accepted that the model has limitations.

rules.title: Adverbs and quantifiers of caution
rules.body: Adverbs fine-tune the strength of a claim: arguably, presumably, apparently, seemingly, largely, broadly, somewhat, to some extent, in most cases, almost certainly. Boosters such as clearly, undoubtedly and obviously do the opposite and should be used sparingly; readers distrust writing that is certain of everything. Place the adverb close to the element it qualifies: 'The effect is largely confined to urban areas.'

examples.target: The effect is largely confined to urban areas.
This is arguably the most important finding.
The decline is, to some extent, seasonal.

rules.title: Formal lexis and verb choice
rules.body: Formal register replaces phrasal verbs with single Latinate verbs (look into → investigate, put off → postpone, find out → ascertain, set up → establish, carry out → conduct, get worse → deteriorate), avoids contractions and vague quantifiers ('a lot of' → 'a great deal of', 'considerable', 'numerous'), and prefers 'obtain' to 'get', 'require' to 'need'. Some phrasal verbs are nevertheless normal in formal prose: carry out, point out, set out, rule out.

examples.target: Further research is needed to confirm these findings.
The study was conducted in 2019.
A great deal of evidence supports this view.
examples.en: a great deal of for a lot of

rules.title: The agentless passive in reporting
rules.body: Methods and results sections use the passive to keep the focus on the procedure: 'Samples were collected at monthly intervals'; 'It was found that ...'. The agent is omitted when it is obvious, unknown or unimportant, and restored with 'by' when it matters: 'The survey was commissioned by the ministry.' Modern style guides accept the first person in discussion sections ('We argue that ...'), so the passive is a choice, not a rule.

examples.target: Samples were collected at monthly intervals.
examples.en: agentless passive in a method description

examples.target: It was found that the effect disappeared after six weeks.
The survey was commissioned by the ministry.

rules.title: Shell nouns and 'the extent to which'
rules.body: Abstract nouns such as issue, approach, notion, claim, assumption, view and finding package an earlier idea for reference: 'This approach raises two further questions'; 'the notion that markets are efficient'. 'The extent to which' and 'the degree to which' introduce a qualified claim: 'The extent to which these results can be generalised is limited.' These devices give academic prose its cohesion and let the writer evaluate without repeating.

examples.target: This approach raises two further questions.
The claim that growth is self-sustaining is questionable.
The extent to which the policy succeeded remains unclear.
examples.en: the extent to which as a subject

rules.title: Calibrating: neither over- nor under-hedged
rules.body: Hedging should match the evidence. Established facts need none ('Water boils at 100 °C at sea level'); interpretations need one clear hedge; speculation needs an explicit marker ('it is possible that', 'one possible explanation is'). Stacking hedges ('it might perhaps possibly be') reads as evasive, while unhedged claims about contested matters ('this proves') read as naive. These findings should be treated with some caution is the model sentence of calibrated academic English.

examples.target: Water boils at 100 °C at sea level.
These findings should be treated with some caution.
One possible explanation is sampling error.

options: The rapid implementation of the policy
The implement of the policy rapidly
exercises.explain: The verb becomes 'implementation', the adverb becomes the adjective 'rapid', the object follows 'of'.

exercises.explain: Verb → noun with -ion.

exercises.explain: Both 'appear to' and 'suggest' soften the claim.
