exercises.en: One could argue that the policy has failed (impersonal frame).

exercises.q: Choose the more academic alternative to 'look into'.
exercises.explain: Formal register prefers the Latinate single verb.

exercises.q: There is considerable ___ that the two events are linked. (noun from 'evident')
exercises.explain: 'There is evidence that' is a standard impersonal frame.

exercises.q: Nominalisation always makes writing clearer.
exercises.explain: Overused, it hides agents and produces abstract, hard-to-read prose.

exercises.q: Which sentence hedges most appropriately?
options: The results suggest a link between the two.
The results prove a link between the two.
The results obviously show a link.
The results definitely establish a link.
exercises.explain: 'Suggest' presents the link as an interpretation of the data.

exercises.q: It is ___ that the reforms were introduced too late. (adjective from 'argue', meaning 'it can be argued')
exercises.explain: 'It is arguable that' is an impersonal hedging frame.

exercises.answer: The failure of the talks was widely attributed to mistrust.
exercises.en: People widely blamed mistrust for the talks failing.

exercises.q: 'A decision was taken to close the plant.' What does the nominalised passive hide?
exercises.explain: The agent of 'decide' is suppressed.

exercises.q: The findings ___ to indicate a seasonal effect. (hedging verb, present tense)
exercises.explain: 'Appear/seem/tend to' present the indication as tentative.

exercises.q: In academic English, 'a lot of' is usually replaced by 'a great deal of' or 'considerable'.
exercises.explain: 'A lot of' is informal; formal prose prefers these alternatives.

exercises.q: Spot the over-hedged sentence.
options: It might perhaps possibly be the case that costs may rise.
It seems likely that costs will rise.
exercises.explain: Four stacked hedges read as evasive; one is enough.

exercises.q: Rewrite as a nominalisation: 'The company expanded rapidly, which worried investors.' → The company's rapid ___ worried investors.
exercises.explain: expand → expansion; the subject becomes a possessive.

exercises.answer: The extent to which the policy succeeded remains unclear.
exercises.en: It is unclear how far the policy succeeded.

exercises.q: It ___ appear that the sample was contaminated.
exercises.explain: 'It would appear' is the tentative inference frame.

exercises.q: Samples ___ collected at monthly intervals. (agentless passive, past)
exercises.explain: The methods passive omits the agent.

exercises.q: 'The notion that' and 'the claim that' are shell nouns that package an earlier idea for reference.
exercises.explain: Shell nouns label a proposition so it can be evaluated.

exercises.q: Which is the best unpacking of 'The utilisation of the facility by staff showed an increase'?
options: The facility had an increase of staff use.
Staff were utilised by the facility more.
exercises.explain: Restoring the agent and the verb gives the plain meaning.

exercises.q: This ___ raises two further questions. (shell noun meaning 'way of tackling a problem')
exercises.explain: 'This approach' refers back to a method just described.

exercises.answer: It is generally accepted that the model has limitations.
exercises.en: Most people agree the model has limitations.

exercises.q: Hedging is unnecessary when stating an established fact such as 'water boils at 100 °C at sea level'.
exercises.explain: Hedge interpretations, not facts.

exercises.q: The ___ to which these results can be generalised is limited. (noun)
exercises.explain: 'The extent/degree to which' introduces a qualified claim.

exercises.q: Choose the sentence in the most appropriate academic register.
options: Further research is needed to confirm these findings.
We need to do loads more research to check this.
Someone should really look into this more.
exercises.explain: Impersonal, unhedged-but-measured and free of informal lexis.

exercises.answer: These findings should be treated with some caution.
exercises.en: Be careful how much weight you give these findings.

exercises.q: Rewrite with a hedging modal: 'This explains the discrepancy.' → This ___ explain the discrepancy. (modal of possibility)
exercises.explain: A single modal turns the assertion into a possibility.

sections.title: Articles, determiners and quantifiers at C2
sections.summary: Article errors are the last to disappear in even the most fluent non-native English. This chapter covers the zero article with abstractions and generic plurals, 'the + adjective' for groups, generic 'the/a/zero', the few/a few contrast, each/every/either/neither, 'whatever/whichever', institutions ('in hospital'), proper names and the quantifier agreement traps ('a number of' vs 'the number of').

rules.title: Zero article with abstractions and generic plurals
rules.body: Uncountable abstract nouns and plural countables take no article when they refer to the idea or the class in general: 'Love is blind'; 'Education matters'; 'Tigers are endangered.' As soon as the noun is specified by a following phrase or by context, 'the' returns: 'the education she received', 'the love of a parent'. The contrast 'Life is short' / 'the life of a miner' is the core of the system.

examples.target: Honesty is the best policy.
The honesty of the witness impressed the jury.
Computers have changed publishing.

rules.title: The + adjective for groups and abstractions
rules.body: 'The' + adjective denotes a whole class of people and takes a plural verb: 'the poor', 'the unemployed', 'the elderly', 'the wealthy', 'the French', 'the Dutch'. It cannot be made plural with -s or used for one person (*a poor, *the poor is). With a few participles it denotes an individual in legal language: 'the accused', 'the deceased' (singular). With other adjectives it names an abstraction: 'the unknown', 'the sublime', 'the unexpected'.

examples.target: The elderly are often the most vulnerable to heat.
The accused was led away.
The unexpected has happened.

rules.title: Generic reference: the tiger, a tiger, tigers
rules.body: A class can be referred to in three ways. 'The' + singular treats the class as a type and is formal or scientific: 'The tiger is a solitary hunter'; it is also used for inventions and instruments: 'the wheel', 'the telephone', 'play the piano'. 'A' + singular means 'any member': 'A tiger will attack if cornered.' The bare plural is the neutral, everyday form: 'Tigers are solitary.' Only 'the' + singular and the plural can be used for statements about the class as a whole ('The tiger is dying out', not *A tiger is dying out).

examples.target: The wheel was one of humanity's earliest inventions.
A doctor will tell you the same.
examples.en: a = any member of the class

examples.target: He plays the violin in an amateur orchestra.

rules.title: Few / a few, little / a little, quite a few
rules.body: 'A few' and 'a little' are positive ('some'); 'few' and 'little' without the article are negative ('hardly any'). 'Quite a few' and 'a good few' mean 'a fairly large number'. 'The few' and 'the little' mean 'the small amount that exists': 'the few who survived'. 'So few / so little' and 'too few / too little' are the quantifier equivalents of 'so/too many'. 'Few' alone is formal; speech prefers 'not many'.

examples.target: He has a few friends, so he is rarely lonely.
He has few friends and is often lonely.
A little patience is needed when training a puppy.
examples.en: a little with an uncountable noun

examples.target: Quite a few people complained.
examples.en: quite a few = a fair number

rules.title: Each, every, either, neither, both, all
rules.body: 'Each' considers members one by one and can apply to two or more; 'every' sees them as a group and needs three or more. Both take a singular noun and verb: 'Each of the players was given a medal'; 'Every student has a tutor.' 'Either' means one of two, or both sides ('on either side of the road'); 'neither' means not one of two and takes a singular verb in formal English: 'Neither of the candidates was willing.' 'Both' and 'all' take plural verbs; 'all (of) the', 'both (of) the' and 'half (of) the' allow 'of' to be dropped before a determiner: 'half the audience'.

examples.target: Each of the players was given a medal.
examples.en: each of + plural noun, singular verb

examples.target: Neither of the candidates was willing to compromise.
There were trees on either side of the road.
Half the audience had left.

rules.title: Whatever, whichever, whoever, however
rules.body: The -ever words have two uses. As free-choice determiners or pronouns they mean 'any ... that': 'Take whichever seat you like' (from a limited set); 'Whatever you decide is fine'; 'Whoever leaves last should lock up.' As concessive conjunctions they mean 'no matter what/which/who/how': 'Whatever it costs, we'll pay'; 'However much it costs, we'll pay.' 'Whichever' is preferred when the choice is among a known set; 'any' is the neutral everyday word with the free-choice sense: 'Any doctor will tell you that.'

examples.target: Take whichever seat you like; they're all free.
examples.en: free choice from a limited set

examples.target: However much it costs, we'll pay.
Whoever leaves last should lock the door.

rules.title: Institutions and fixed phrases without the article
rules.body: When a building is referred to for its purpose, British English drops the article: in hospital, at school, in prison, to church, in bed, at sea, at work, by car, on foot. With 'the', the reference is to the place as a building: 'She went to the church to see the frescoes.' American English keeps 'the' with hospital ('in the hospital'). 'The' is obligatory with superlatives, ordinals and unique nouns ('the first', 'the sun'), while 'a most + adjective' means 'a very ...', not a superlative.

examples.target: She was taken to hospital with a broken arm.
The children are at school until three.
It was a most interesting lecture.

rules.title: Articles with proper names
rules.body: Rivers, seas, oceans, mountain ranges, deserts, plural countries and island groups take 'the': the Thames, the Pacific, the Alps, the Sahara, the Netherlands, the Philippines. Single mountains, lakes, cities, continents and most countries take none: Mount Everest, Lake Geneva, Europe, France. Newspapers, organisations with 'of' and families in the plural take 'the': the Times, the University of Leeds, the Smiths. 'A' before a surname means 'a certain' or 'a work by': 'a Mr Jones', 'a Picasso'.

examples.target: The Thames flows through London.
Lake Geneva lies between Switzerland and France.
The Netherlands and the Alps both take the article.
A Mr Jones called while you were out.

rules.title: Quantifier agreement traps
rules.body: 'A number of' + plural noun takes a plural verb ('A number of applicants have withdrawn'), while 'the number of' is singular ('The number of applicants has fallen'). 'A great deal of' and 'much' go with uncountables, 'several' and 'many' with plurals. 'Most people' is generic but 'most of the people' is specific. 'None of' takes a singular verb in formal style and a plural informally. 'Any' in affirmatives means 'whichever': 'Any doctor will tell you.'

examples.target: A number of applicants have withdrawn.
The number of applicants has fallen.
Most people prefer the original.

rules.title: The with comparatives and other fixed determiner patterns
rules.body: 'The' + comparative ... 'the' + comparative links two variables: 'The more I read, the less I understand.' 'The same', 'the former', 'the latter' and 'the following' always take 'the'. 'Such a', 'what a', 'rather a' and 'quite a' put the article after the first word before a singular countable: 'such a mess', 'what a day'. 'Not every' and 'not all' are the standard partial negatives: 'Not every student is suited to academic study.'

examples.target: The more I read about it, the less I understand.
What a day it has been!
Not every student is suited to academic study.

exercises.q: ___ honesty is the best policy.
exercises.explain: A generic abstract noun takes the zero article.

exercises.q: The government has promised more help for ___ unemployed. (article)
exercises.explain: 'The' + adjective refers to the group as a whole.

exercises.q: 'The French are proud of their cuisine' uses 'the + adjective' to refer to a whole nation.
exercises.explain: Nationality adjectives with 'the' denote the people as a group, with a plural verb.

exercises.answer: The elderly are often the most vulnerable to heat.
exercises.en: Old people are often the most at risk in heat.

exercises.q: ___ of the two routes is faster; take whichever you prefer.
exercises.explain: 'Neither' is used for two items; 'none' needs three or more.

exercises.q: There were ___ people at the concert that it was cancelled. (two words meaning 'such a small number of')
exercises.explain: 'So few' + plural is the quantifier equivalent of 'so many'.

exercises.q: 'Each' can be used with two or more items, but 'every' needs three or more.
exercises.explain: You can say 'each of the two' but not 'every one of the two'.

exercises.q: ___ wheel was one of humanity's earliest inventions.
exercises.explain: 'The' + singular names an invention as a type.

exercises.q: Take ___ seat you like; they're all free. (determiner meaning 'any one that')
exercises.explain: Free-choice 'whichever' (from a set), 'whatever' or 'any' all fit.

exercises.answer: The more I read about it, the less I understand.
exercises.en: Reading more only makes me understand less.

exercises.q: She was taken to ___ hospital with a broken arm. (British English)
exercises.explain: British English drops the article when the institution's purpose is meant.

exercises.q: He plays ___ violin in an amateur orchestra. (article)
exercises.explain: Musical instruments take 'the' after 'play'.

exercises.q: 'The number of students have increased' is correct.
exercises.explain: 'The number of' is singular: 'has increased'.

exercises.q: Spot the error.
options: The poor is always with us.
exercises.explain: 'The poor' denotes a group and takes a plural verb: 'are'.

exercises.q: ___ much it costs, we'll pay. (concessive wh-word)
exercises.explain: 'However much' = no matter how much.

exercises.answer: Neither of the candidates was willing to compromise.
exercises.en: Not one of the two candidates would compromise.

exercises.q: Which is correct?
options: The half of audience had left.
exercises.explain: 'Half' is followed directly by 'the' + noun; 'of' is optional.

exercises.q: We walked along the river, with trees on ___ side. (determiner meaning 'both')
exercises.explain: 'On either side' = on both sides.

exercises.q: 'A most interesting lecture' means 'the most interesting lecture'.
exercises.explain: 'A most' + adjective means 'a very ...', not a superlative.

exercises.q: ___ Netherlands and ___ Alps both take the definite article.
exercises.explain: Plural country names and mountain ranges take 'the'.

exercises.q: ___ patience is needed when training a puppy. (two words, positive sense 'some')
exercises.explain: 'A little' is positive; 'little' alone would mean 'hardly any'.

exercises.answer: Whoever leaves last should lock the door.
exercises.en: The last person to leave should lock the door.

exercises.q: Each of the players ___ given a medal.
exercises.explain: 'Each of' takes a singular verb.

exercises.q: 'She has gone to the church to pray' is the normal way to say she is attending a service.
exercises.explain: For the purpose of worship it is 'gone to church'; 'the church' refers to the building.

exercises.q: Rewrite with 'the + adjective': 'People who are wealthy pay more tax.' → ___ pay more tax. (two words)
exercises.explain: 'The' + adjective replaces 'people who are ...'.

exercises.q: Which sentence uses 'any' to mean 'whichever'?
options: Any doctor will tell you that.
exercises.explain: In an affirmative statement 'any' means 'it doesn't matter which'.

exercises.answer: Not every student is suited to academic study.
exercises.en: Some students are not suited to academic study.

exercises.q: He has ___ friends, so he is rarely lonely. (quantifier, two words, positive)
exercises.explain: 'A few' is positive ('some'); 'few' would mean the opposite.

exercises.q: In 'Love is blind', the zero article gives 'love' a generic, abstract meaning.
exercises.explain: Abstract nouns used generically take no article.

sections.title: Relative clauses, prepositions and the formal whom/which
sections.summary: Formal English keeps 'whom' for objects, moves prepositions in front of the relative pronoun ('the house in which I grew up'), uses 'of which' and 'whose', and comments on whole clauses with 'which', 'in which case' and 'by which time'. This chapter covers these choices, the defining/non-defining contrast and the quantifier + 'of whom/which' pattern.

rules.title: Whom: object of a verb or preposition
rules.body: 'Whom' is the object form of 'who' and is used in formal style when the pronoun is the object of the relative clause or of a preposition: 'the colleague whom I met', 'the colleague to whom I spoke'. It is obligatory directly after a preposition ('to whom', 'with whom'), where 'who' is impossible. It must never be the subject: *'the man whom is in charge'. A parenthetical 'you think' or 'they say' does not change the case: 'the official who you think is responsible'.

examples.target: The colleague to whom I spoke has resigned.
Several people, most of whom I knew, were waiting.
Ask the official who you think is responsible.

rules.title: Pied-piping versus preposition stranding
rules.body: A preposition belonging to the relative clause can stay at the end (stranding: 'the house I grew up in') or move in front of the pronoun (pied-piping: 'the house in which I grew up'). Formal writing prefers pied-piping, which requires 'which' or 'whom', never 'that' or a zero pronoun (*'in that I grew up'). Stranding is normal in speech and with 'that' or no pronoun. Complex prepositions pied-pipe as a unit: 'the theory according to which markets are efficient'.

examples.target: The house in which I grew up has been sold.
This is the pen I was looking for.
The manner in which the news was announced upset many.
The theory according to which markets are efficient is contested.

rules.title: Whose and of which
rules.body: 'Whose' expresses possession for people and, in modern usage, for things: 'a writer whose novels are banned', 'a car whose engine had failed'. The formal alternative for things is 'of which', placed after the noun ('the building, the roof of which collapsed') or before it ('of which the roof collapsed'). 'Of which' is also the normal form after quantifiers: 'the conclusions, some of which were leaked'.

examples.target: A writer whose novels are banned has won the prize.
The building, the roof of which collapsed, was condemned.
The report, the conclusions of which were leaked, was withdrawn.
examples.en: of which in a non-defining clause

rules.title: Sentential relatives and fixed which-phrases
rules.body: 'Which' after a comma can refer to a whole preceding clause: 'He failed the test, which surprised nobody.' Fixed phrases built on this pattern link a condition or time to what follows: 'in which case' (if that happens), 'by which time' (before that moment), 'at which point' (then), 'as a result of which', 'in spite of which', 'whereupon' (immediately after which). They are typical of formal narrative and legal prose.

examples.target: He failed the test, which surprised nobody.
examples.en: which refers to the whole clause

examples.target: He may be late, in which case we will start without him.
examples.en: in which case = if that happens

examples.target: We arrived at noon, by which time the shop had closed.
The deadline passed, whereupon the offer was withdrawn.

rules.title: Defining versus non-defining clauses
rules.body: A defining clause identifies which one is meant and has no commas: 'My brother who lives in Leeds is a vet' (I have more than one brother). A non-defining clause adds information about an already identified noun and is enclosed in commas: 'My brother, who lives in Leeds, is a vet' (my only brother). 'That' and the zero pronoun occur only in defining clauses; non-defining clauses need 'who', 'whom', 'whose' or 'which'. In American style, 'that' is preferred for defining and 'which' reserved for non-defining.

examples.target: The film that won was French.
The film, which won, was French.
My brother, who lives in Leeds, is a vet.

rules.title: Quantifier + of whom / of which
rules.body: A non-defining clause can begin with a quantifier or number followed by 'of whom' (people) or 'of which' (things): 'She has three sons, all of whom are doctors'; 'Several witnesses, none of whom agreed, were called'; 'the last of which', 'the majority of which'. The verb agrees with the quantifier: 'none of whom was/were', 'each of which is'. This pattern replaces a clumsy second sentence ('... and all of them are doctors').

examples.target: She has three sons, all of whom are doctors.
Several witnesses, none of whom agreed, were called.
The committee, most of whom were new, approved the plan.

rules.title: Relative adverbs and formal where-compounds
rules.body: 'Where' stands for 'in/at which', 'when' for 'on/at which', 'why' for 'for which': 'the day when (on which) we met'. Formal and legal English adds 'whereby' (by means of which: 'a scheme whereby staff buy shares'), 'wherein' (in which), 'whereupon' (after which) and 'whereas' (which, by contrast, is a conjunction, not a relative). 'The extent to which' and 'the way in which' are standard formal frames.

examples.target: The company introduced a scheme whereby staff could buy shares.
The day on which we met was wet.
The extent to which this is true is debatable.

rules.title: Phrasal verbs and prepositions that cannot move
rules.body: The particle of a phrasal verb cannot be pied-piped: 'the problem which we put up with' is possible, but *'the problem up with which we put' is not, and 'the problem with which we put up' is awkward at best. Prepositions in fixed idioms and in prepositional verbs behave the same way: 'the colleague I rely on' pied-pipes acceptably ('on whom I rely'), but 'the tune I was humming along to' does not. When pied-piping sounds strained, rewrite with stranding or a different verb.

examples.target: The noise which we put up with was constant.
The people on whom we relied let us down.
The tools with which she worked were antique.

rules.title: Prepositions in infinitive relatives
rules.body: A to-infinitive can act as a reduced relative with a stranded preposition: 'someone to talk to', 'a chair to sit on'. In formal style the preposition moves in front of 'which' or 'whom' and the infinitive follows: 'a pen with which to sign', 'someone in whom to confide', 'the means by which to achieve it'. The formal form requires an explicit pronoun; *'a pen with to write' is impossible.

examples.target: She gave me a pen with which to sign the form.
I need someone in whom I can confide.
examples.en: in whom with a finite clause

examples.target: He has nobody to talk to.
examples.en: stranded preposition in an infinitive relative

exercises.q: The colleague ___ I spoke yesterday has resigned. (formal)
exercises.explain: After a preposition the object form 'whom' is obligatory.

exercises.q: The house ___ which I grew up has been sold. (preposition)
exercises.explain: The preposition of 'grow up in' is pied-piped before 'which'.

exercises.q: 'Whom' can be used as the subject of a relative clause, as in 'the man whom came'.
exercises.explain: 'Whom' is only an object form; the subject is 'who'.

exercises.answer: The committee, most of whom were new, approved the plan.
exercises.en: The committee, mostly new members, approved the plan.

exercises.q: Which sentence strands the preposition?
options: This is the pen I was looking for.
This is the pen for which I was looking.
This is the pen which for I was looking.
This is for the pen which I was looking.
exercises.explain: The preposition stays at the end of the clause.

exercises.q: She has three sons, all ___ whom are doctors.
exercises.explain: Quantifier + 'of whom' opens a non-defining clause.

exercises.q: In a non-defining relative clause, 'that' can replace 'which'.
exercises.explain: 'That' is restricted to defining clauses.

exercises.q: The company introduced a scheme ___ staff could buy shares at a discount.
exercises.explain: 'Whereby' = by means of which.

exercises.q: Rewrite formally: 'the author the book is dedicated to' → the author ___ the book is dedicated (two words)
exercises.explain: Pied-piping requires 'whom' after the preposition.

exercises.answer: He failed the test, which surprised nobody.
exercises.en: Nobody was surprised that he failed (sentential relative).

exercises.q: Spot the error.
options: The tools with which she worked were antique.
The problem up with which we put was serious.
The people on whom we relied let us down.
The day on which we met was wet.
exercises.explain: A phrasal-verb particle cannot be pied-piped; say 'the problem which we put up with'.

exercises.q: The building, the roof ___ which collapsed, was condemned.
exercises.explain: Noun + 'of which' is the formal possessive for things.

exercises.q: 'A car whose engine had failed' is acceptable: 'whose' can refer to things.
exercises.explain: Modern usage allows 'whose' for inanimates; 'of which' is the formal alternative.

exercises.q: He may be late, ___ we will start without him.
exercises.explain: 'In which case' links a possible situation to its consequence.

exercises.q: The manner ___ which the news was announced upset many.
exercises.explain: 'The manner in which' is a fixed formal frame.

exercises.answer: The report, the conclusions of which were leaked, was withdrawn.
exercises.en: The report whose conclusions were leaked was withdrawn.

exercises.q: Which is the most formal version?
options: The person to whom you should write is the registrar.
The person who you should write to is the registrar.
The person you should write to is the registrar.
The person that you should write to is the registrar.
exercises.explain: Pied-piping with 'whom' is the most formal option.

exercises.q: Several witnesses, none ___ whom agreed, were called.
exercises.explain: 'None of whom' opens the non-defining clause.

exercises.q: 'The theory according to which markets are efficient' pied-pipes a complex preposition.
exercises.explain: 'According to' moves as a unit in front of 'which'.

exercises.q: The deadline passed, ___ the offer was withdrawn.
exercises.explain: 'Whereupon' = immediately after which.

exercises.q: I need someone ___ whom I can confide. (preposition)
exercises.explain: 'Confide in' pied-pipes as 'in whom'.

exercises.answer: We arrived at noon, by which time the shop had closed.
exercises.en: By the time we arrived at noon, the shop had closed.

exercises.q: Which sentence contains a sentential relative?
options: The train was late, which meant we missed the connection.
The train, which was late, was crowded.
The train which was late was crowded.
The train that was late was crowded.
exercises.explain: 'Which' refers to the whole fact that the train was late.

exercises.q: Rewrite with 'whose': 'a writer the novels of whom are banned' → a writer ___ novels are banned
exercises.explain: 'Whose' is the neutral possessive relative.

exercises.q: 'The man whom is in charge' is correct because 'whom' is formal.
exercises.explain: 'Whom' is an object form; the subject needs 'who'.

pairs: My brother who lives in Leeds is a vet.
defining: I have more than one brother
My brother, who lives in Leeds, is a vet.
The film that won was French.
The film, which won, was French.

exercises.answer: She gave me a pen with which to sign the form.
exercises.en: She gave me a pen to sign the form with.

exercises.q: The extent ___ which this is true is debatable. (preposition)
exercises.explain: 'The extent to which' is the fixed formal frame.

exercises.q: Choose the correct pronoun: 'Ask the official ___ you think is responsible.'
exercises.explain: The pronoun is the subject of 'is responsible'; 'you think' is parenthetical.

sections.title: Phrasal verbs, multi-word verbs and particle placement
sections.summary: Multi-word verbs are where fluent speakers still stumble: whether the particle can be separated from the verb, where a pronoun object goes, how three-part verbs like 'put up with' behave, and when a Latinate verb should replace the phrasal verb in formal writing. This chapter sets out the four structural types, the placement rules, the core meanings of the particles and the register choices.

rules.title: Four types of multi-word verb
rules.body: (1) Intransitive phrasal verbs take no object: 'The car broke down.' (2) Transitive phrasal verbs take an object that can go on either side of the particle: 'turn off the light / turn the light off'. (3) Prepositional verbs are inseparable, with the object always after the preposition: 'look after the children'. (4) Phrasal-prepositional (three-part) verbs combine a particle and a preposition, with the object at the end: 'put up with the noise'. Knowing the type of each verb is what makes placement automatic.

examples.target: The plane took off on time.
She looked the word up. / She looked up the word.
Who is looking after the children?
I can't put up with this noise.
examples.en: three-part verb, object at the end

rules.title: Particle placement with separable verbs
rules.body: With a noun object both orders are possible: 'hand in the essay / hand the essay in'. With a pronoun object the particle must follow the pronoun: 'hand it in', never *hand in it. With a long or heavy object the particle normally comes first so that the object closes the sentence: 'She turned down the first three offers she received.' Putting a long object between verb and particle is grammatical but hard to process.

examples.target: Turn it off. (not *Turn off it.)
examples.en: pronoun object must precede the particle

examples.target: Please fill in this form. / Please fill this form in.
She turned down the first three offers she received.

rules.title: Inseparable prepositional verbs and stress
rules.body: In a prepositional verb such as look after, look at, deal with, rely on, run into or come across, the object always follows the preposition and can never go between: *'look the children after'. In speech the preposition is unstressed ('look AT it'), whereas the particle of a phrasal verb carries stress ('look it UP'); this distinction is a reliable test. Prepositional verbs can be made passive with the preposition stranded: 'The children were looked after.'

examples.target: We ran into an old friend at the station.
examples.en: inseparable: run into = meet by chance

examples.target: I came across this word in a novel.
The matter is being looked into by the police.

rules.title: Three-part verbs
rules.body: Phrasal-prepositional verbs have a particle followed by a preposition and are never split: put up with (tolerate), look forward to, get away with, come up with (produce an idea), run out of, look down on, look up to, catch up on, cut down on, get round to, face up to, live up to, get on with. The object comes after the whole unit, and a following verb takes the -ing form because 'to' is a preposition: 'I look forward to seeing you'; 'He never got round to painting the fence.'

examples.target: She came up with a brilliant solution.
I'm looking forward to seeing you next week.
He never got round to painting the fence.
Nobody expected the company to live up to its reputation.

rules.title: Multi-word verbs in passives and relative clauses
rules.body: Multi-word verbs keep their particle or preposition in the passive and in relative clauses: 'The meeting was called off'; 'the offer which we turned down'; 'a problem to be dealt with'. The preposition of a prepositional verb is stranded, not moved in front of the pronoun, unless the style is very formal ('the colleague on whom I rely'); with a phrasal-verb particle, fronting is impossible (*'up with which we put', see chapter 8).

examples.target: The meeting was called off at the last minute.
The offer which we turned down last year has been renewed.
examples.en: particle stays in the relative clause

examples.target: The children were brought up by their grandparents.
examples.en: passive of bring up with by-agent

rules.title: Register: phrasal verb or Latinate verb?
rules.body: Most phrasal verbs are neutral to informal, and formal writing often replaces them with single Latinate verbs: put off → postpone, bring about → cause, carry out → conduct, look into → investigate, set up → establish, turn down → reject, call off → cancel, find out → ascertain/discover, give up → abandon, take on → employ/assume. The substitution is a tendency, not a rule: 'set up', 'carry out', 'point out' and 'rule out' are perfectly at home in academic prose, and forcing a Latinate verb everywhere sounds pompous.

examples.target: The study was conducted in 2019.
The committee set up a working group.
examples.en: set up is acceptable in formal style

examples.target: The proposal was rejected.

rules.title: Polysemy: one verb, many meanings
rules.body: A single phrasal verb can have several unrelated meanings, literal and figurative. 'Take off' can mean to leave the ground, to remove clothing, to succeed suddenly, to imitate someone, or to deduct. 'Make out' can mean to discern, to claim falsely, to write a cheque or to kiss. 'Put down' can mean to place, to write, to humiliate or to have an animal killed. Context and the type of object disambiguate; learn each sense as a separate item with its own collocations.

examples.target: Sales took off after the advert.
I can't make out what the sign says.
She put him down in front of everyone.

rules.title: Core meanings of the particles
rules.body: Particles carry recurring meanings that make new combinations guessable. 'Up' often means completion or increase (eat up, use up, speed up); 'out' exhaustion or distribution (die out, sell out, hand out); 'on' continuation (carry on, keep on); 'off' departure or termination (set off, call off); 'down' decrease or recording (slow down, note down); 'back' return (give back, call back); 'over' repetition or transfer (do over, hand over); 'through' completion of a process (see through, get through).

examples.target: We have run out of time.
Carry on without me.
She cut down on sugar and gave up smoking.
Give it back to me at once.

rules.title: Nouns and adjectives from phrasal verbs
rules.body: Many phrasal verbs have a noun counterpart written as one word or hyphenated, with the stress on the first element: breakdown, setback, takeover, outbreak, upbringing, let-down, drop-out, check-in. Some reverse the order (outbreak, upbringing, input). Participial adjectives follow the same pattern: 'a worn-out carpet', 'a made-up story', 'a run-down area'. The verb itself is never written as one word: 'to break down', not *to breakdown.

examples.target: The sudden breakdown of the talks shocked the markets.
The merger was a setback for the regulator.
His strict upbringing shaped his character.

exercises.q: Which is correct?
exercises.explain: A pronoun object must come between the verb and the particle.

exercises.q: I'm looking forward to ___ you next week. (verb 'see')
exercises.explain: 'To' in 'look forward to' is a preposition, so the -ing form follows.

exercises.q: 'Look after' is separable: 'look the children after' is correct.
exercises.explain: 'Look after' is a prepositional verb; the object always follows 'after'.

exercises.answer: She came up with a brilliant solution to the problem.
exercises.en: She produced a brilliant solution to the problem.

exercises.q: The plane ___ on time.
exercises.explain: 'Take off' (leave the ground) is intransitive here.

exercises.q: He never got round to ___ the fence. (verb 'paint')
exercises.explain: 'Get round to' ends in the preposition 'to', so -ing follows.

exercises.q: With a long noun-phrase object, the particle usually comes before the object: 'She turned down the first three offers she received.'
exercises.explain: End-weight keeps the heavy object at the end of the sentence.

exercises.q: Which sentence is wrong?
options: I can't put up with this noise.
I can't put this noise up with.
exercises.explain: Three-part verbs are never split; the object follows 'with'.

exercises.q: The matter is being looked ___ by the police. (particle)
exercises.explain: 'Look into' = investigate; the preposition stays in the passive.

exercises.answer: The meeting was called off at the last minute.
exercises.en: The meeting was cancelled at the last minute.

exercises.q: In formal writing, 'The committee set up a working group' is:
options: acceptable: set up is neutral even in formal style
wrong: phrasal verbs are forbidden in formal writing
exercises.explain: Some phrasal verbs, including 'set up', are standard in formal prose.

exercises.q: Nobody expected the company to live ___ its reputation. (two words)
exercises.explain: 'Live up to' = be as good as expected.

exercises.q: 'Take off' can mean to leave the ground, to remove clothing, to succeed suddenly and to imitate someone.
exercises.explain: Phrasal verbs are often polysemous; context decides the sense.

exercises.q: Give ___ at once.
exercises.explain: Pronoun object before the particle, then the to-phrase.

exercises.q: The sudden ___ of the talks shocked the markets. (noun from 'break down')
exercises.explain: The noun is written as one word, stressed on the first syllable.

exercises.answer: We have run out of time and must stop here.
exercises.en: Our time is exhausted, so we must stop.

exercises.q: Choose the formal equivalent of 'find out'.
exercises.explain: 'Ascertain' (or 'discover') is the Latinate alternative.

exercises.q: She gets ___ with murder because the boss likes her. (particle)
exercises.explain: 'Get away with' = escape punishment for.

exercises.q: In 'look at the picture', 'at' is stressed in speech, just as 'up' is in 'look it up'.
exercises.explain: Prepositions in prepositional verbs are unstressed; phrasal-verb particles are stressed.

exercises.q: Which pair shows a separable verb with a noun object in both possible positions?
options: hand in the essay / hand the essay in
get over the shock / get the shock over
run into a friend / run a friend into
come across a word / come a word across
exercises.explain: 'Hand in' is separable; the others are inseparable prepositional verbs.

exercises.q: The children were brought ___ by their grandparents. (particle)
exercises.explain: 'Bring up' = raise; the particle stays in the passive.

exercises.answer: The offer which we turned down last year has been renewed.
exercises.en: The offer we rejected last year has been made again.

pairs: a sudden start of disease or war

exercises.q: I can't make ___ what the sign says.
exercises.explain: 'Make out' = discern, manage to see or read.

exercises.q: Rewrite with a phrasal verb: 'He tolerates her moods.' → He puts ___ her moods. (two words)
exercises.explain: 'Put up with' = tolerate.

exercises.q: 'Look down on' and 'look up to' are three-part verbs whose object always follows the preposition.
exercises.explain: Phrasal-prepositional verbs are never split.

exercises.answer: She cut down on sugar and gave up smoking entirely.
exercises.en: She reduced her sugar intake and stopped smoking completely.

exercises.q: Spot the error.
exercises.explain: A pronoun object cannot follow the particle of a separable verb.

exercises.q: Rewrite in a formal register: 'The study was carried out in 2019.' → The study was ___ in 2019. (one Latinate verb)
exercises.explain: 'Conduct', 'undertake' and 'perform' are the formal equivalents of 'carry out'.

sections.title: Punctuation, cohesion and discourse
sections.summary: Native-like writing is held together by punctuation that signals structure (semicolons, colons, dashes), by linking devices chosen for their function, and by ellipsis and substitution that avoid repetition ('so do I', 'I hope so', 'the former / the latter'). This chapter covers those devices and the comma splice, the error most editors notice first.

rules.title: Semicolons
rules.body: A semicolon joins two independent clauses that are closely related in meaning without a conjunction: 'The results were clear; the committee acted at once.' It is required before a conjunctive adverb (however, therefore, moreover, nevertheless, consequently) that links two clauses: 'The plan was expensive; moreover, it was unpopular.' It also separates items in a list when the items themselves contain commas. It is not used before 'and', 'but' or a subordinate clause.

examples.target: The results were clear; the committee acted at once.
The plan was expensive; moreover, it was unpopular.
Delegates came from Lyon, France; Turin, Italy; and Basel, Switzerland.

rules.title: Colons
rules.body: A colon follows a complete clause and introduces what explains, lists or exemplifies it: 'She needed three things: time, money and luck.' What follows the colon may be a word, a list, a clause or a quotation. A colon must not separate a verb from its object or a preposition from its complement (*'She needed: time, money'), and it does not follow 'such as', 'including' or 'for example'. A capital letter after a colon is American practice when a full sentence follows.

examples.target: She needed three things: time, money and luck.
examples.en: colon introducing a list after a complete clause

examples.target: There was one problem: nobody had a key.
She needed time, money and luck.
examples.en: no colon between verb and object

rules.title: Dashes and parentheses
rules.body: A pair of dashes (em dashes closed up in American style, spaced en dashes in British style) marks an interruption or an aside with more emphasis than commas: 'The plan – if we can call it that – was abandoned.' A single dash introduces an afterthought or a dramatic conclusion. Parentheses (round brackets) downplay the aside instead. Whichever pair is chosen, both halves must be present, and the sentence must still read correctly if the aside is removed.

examples.target: The plan – if we can call it that – was abandoned.
examples.en: paired dashes for an emphatic aside

examples.target: He had one hobby – arguing.
examples.en: single dash before a dramatic conclusion

examples.target: The figures (see Table 2) are provisional.

rules.title: Comma splices and run-on sentences
rules.body: Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone: *'The train was late, we missed the show.' Fix a comma splice with a full stop, a semicolon, a coordinating conjunction ('so') or by subordinating one clause ('Because the train was late ...'). Conjunctive adverbs do not rescue a splice: *'I was tired, however, I kept working' needs a semicolon or full stop before 'however'. Commas are correct around a non-defining relative clause and before a coordinating conjunction joining clauses.

examples.target: The train was late; we missed the show.
I was tired; however, I kept working.
My sister, who lives in Rome, is visiting.

rules.title: Linking devices by function
rules.body: Choose linkers by the job they do. Addition: moreover, furthermore, in addition, what is more. Contrast: however, nevertheless, nonetheless, on the other hand, conversely. Concession (granting a point before countering it): admittedly, granted, of course. Result: consequently, therefore, hence, thus, as a result. Exemplification: for instance, for example, notably. Clarification: that is, namely, i.e. (not e.g.). Summary: in short, to sum up, in conclusion. Over-signposting weakens prose; one linker per sentence is plenty.

examples.target: The data were incomplete; consequently, the conclusions must be treated with caution.
Admittedly, the scheme is costly; nonetheless, it is necessary.
The report is due on Friday, i.e. the end of the week.

rules.title: Conjunction or adverb? Despite, although, however, whereas
rules.body: Subordinating conjunctions ('although', 'whereas', 'while', 'because') join a clause inside the same sentence; conjunctive adverbs ('however', 'therefore', 'moreover') cannot join clauses and need a full stop or semicolon. 'Despite' and 'in spite of' are prepositions and take a noun or -ing form: 'despite the rain', 'despite being tired', or 'despite the fact that' + clause. 'Whereas' expresses a balanced contrast between two facts, not a concession.

examples.target: Although it rained, we went out.
Despite the rain, we went out.
It rained. However, we went out.
She likes jazz, whereas he prefers opera.

rules.title: Substitution: so, not, do so, one
rules.body: 'So' and 'not' replace a whole clause after think, hope, suppose, expect, be afraid, guess: 'I hope so'; 'I'm afraid not'; 'If so, ...'; 'If not, ...'. 'Do so' replaces a verb phrase: 'She promised to help, and she did so.' 'One/ones' replaces a countable noun: 'I'd like the blue one.' Agreement and addition use so/nor/neither + auxiliary + subject: 'So do I'; 'Neither can he'; 'I enjoy opera, and so does my wife.'

examples.target: Is the shop open? — I hope so.
Did you lock the door? — I'm afraid not.
She promised to help, and she did so.
examples.en: do so replaces the verb phrase

examples.target: I enjoy opera, and so does my wife.

rules.title: Ellipsis
rules.body: Repeated elements are omitted after an auxiliary or modal: 'I can't attend, but my colleague can'; 'She said she'd help, and she has.' The auxiliary must match the omitted form; with 'be' or 'have' it may need to be inserted: 'He is ready and so am I.' Ellipsis also operates in coordinated phrases ('tea and coffee were served') and in comparatives ('older than I thought'). It is a mark of fluent, economical English; repeating the full verb phrase sounds laboured.

examples.target: I can't attend the meeting, but my colleague can.
examples.en: verb phrase omitted after the modal

examples.target: She said she would help, and she has.
He has never apologised, nor has he shown any remorse.

rules.title: Reference: the former, the latter, respectively, this/such
rules.body: 'The former' and 'the latter' refer back to the first and second of exactly two items: 'Tea and coffee were served; the latter was more popular.' With three or more items use 'the first', 'the last'. 'Respectively' pairs two lists in order: 'Smith and Jones were born in 1950 and 1962 respectively.' 'This', 'that', 'these' and 'such' refer to earlier text and are clearer when attached to a noun: 'This policy ...' rather than a bare 'This ...'.

examples.target: Tea and coffee were served; the latter was more popular.
examples.en: the latter = the second of two

examples.target: Smith and Jones were born in 1950 and 1962 respectively.
Such measures are rarely popular.

rules.title: Theme, end-weight and topic shifters
rules.body: English prefers given information at the start of a sentence and new or heavy information at the end; that is why clefts, passives and inversion exist (chapters 1 and 2). Topic shifters announce a change of subject: 'as regards', 'with regard to', 'regarding', 'as for', 'turning to'. Parenthetical comment phrases ('on the whole', 'to be fair', 'in my view') are set off by commas and should not stack. Together with lexical chains (repeating or paraphrasing key nouns), these devices make a text cohere.

examples.target: As regards the budget, nothing has been decided.
The results were, on the whole, encouraging.
If so, we will need to revise the budget.
examples.en: if so links back to the previous sentence

exercises.q: Which sentence uses the semicolon correctly?
options: The results were clear; the committee acted at once.
The results were clear; and the committee acted.
The results; were clear and the committee acted.
The results were clear; because the committee acted.
exercises.explain: A semicolon joins two independent clauses without a conjunction.

exercises.q: 'I was tired, however, I kept working' is correctly punctuated.
exercises.explain: 'However' is an adverb, not a conjunction; this is a comma splice.

exercises.q: I don't think the shop is open, but I hope ___. (clause substitute)
exercises.explain: 'So' replaces the clause 'that it is open'.

exercises.answer: The plan was expensive; moreover, it was unpopular.
exercises.en: The plan was expensive and also unpopular.

exercises.q: Choose the correct use of the colon.
options: She needed three things: time, money and luck.
She needed: time, money and luck.
She needed three things such as: time, money and luck.
She needed three things, : time, money and luck.
exercises.explain: The colon follows a complete clause and introduces the list.

exercises.q: 'Did you remember to lock the door?' 'I'm afraid I didn't remember to lock the door.' → Rewrite the answer with a substitute: I'm afraid ___.
exercises.explain: 'Not' replaces the whole negative clause after 'I'm afraid'.

exercises.q: A colon can follow 'such as' to introduce a list.
exercises.explain: 'Such as' already introduces the examples; no colon is used.

exercises.q: Tea and coffee were served; ___ was more popular.

exercises.q: She works long hours; ___, she rarely takes a holiday. (adverb of addition)
exercises.explain: An addition linker follows the semicolon and is set off by a comma.

exercises.answer: I can't attend the meeting, but my colleague can.
exercises.en: I can't attend the meeting, but my colleague is able to (ellipsis).

pairs: adverb: new sentence or after a semicolon

exercises.q: Spot the comma splice.
options: The train was late, we missed the show.
The train was late, so we missed the show.
The train was late; we missed the show.
Because the train was late, we missed the show.
exercises.explain: Two independent clauses are joined by a comma alone.

exercises.q: The CEO and the CFO were questioned; the ___ was later charged. (reference to the second of two)
exercises.explain: 'The latter' = the CFO, the second item mentioned.

exercises.q: 'The former' refers to the second of two items mentioned.
exercises.explain: 'The former' is the first; 'the latter' is the second.

exercises.q: Which sentence uses dashes correctly?
options: The plan – if we can call it that – was abandoned.
The plan – if we can call it that, was abandoned.
The – plan if we can call it that – was abandoned.
The plan if we can call it that – was abandoned.
exercises.explain: Paired dashes enclose the aside, and the sentence reads correctly without it.

exercises.q: Rewrite with 'so': 'I enjoy opera, and my wife enjoys opera too.' → I enjoy opera, and so ___ my wife. (one word)
exercises.explain: 'So' + auxiliary + subject; the auxiliary matches the present simple.

exercises.answer: If so, we will need to revise the budget.
exercises.en: If that is the case, we must revise the budget.

exercises.q: Choose the correct linker: 'The data were incomplete; ___, the conclusions must be treated with caution.'
exercises.explain: The second clause is a result of the first.

exercises.q: The two authors, Smith and Jones, were born in 1950 and 1962 ___. (adverb meaning 'in that order')
exercises.explain: 'Respectively' pairs the names with the dates in order.

exercises.q: 'If not' can stand for a whole negative conditional clause, as in 'Is it ready? If not, wait.'
exercises.explain: 'Not' substitutes for 'it is not ready'.

pairs: She said she'd help, and she did so.
do so as a verb-phrase substitute
He can swim but I can't.

exercises.q: Which linker signals concession before a counter-argument?
exercises.explain: 'Admittedly' grants a point that will then be countered.

exercises.q: ___ regards the budget, nothing has been decided. (one word, topic shifter)
exercises.explain: 'As regards' introduces a new topic.

exercises.answer: Granted, the scheme is costly; nonetheless, it is necessary.
exercises.en: Yes, the scheme is costly, but it is still necessary.

exercises.q: In 'The report is due on Friday, i.e. the end of the week', 'i.e.' means 'for example'.
exercises.explain: 'i.e.' means 'that is'; 'e.g.' means 'for example'.

exercises.q: Which sentence is best punctuated?
options: My sister, who lives in Rome, is visiting.
My sister who lives in Rome, is visiting.
My sister, who lives in Rome is visiting.
My sister who, lives in Rome is visiting.
exercises.explain: A non-defining relative clause is enclosed by a pair of commas.

exercises.q: He has never apologised, ___ has he shown any remorse. (negative additive; inversion follows)
exercises.explain: 'Nor/neither' + auxiliary + subject adds a second negative.

exercises.answer: The results were, on the whole, encouraging.
exercises.en: Overall, the results were encouraging.

exercises.q: Spot the error in cohesion.
options: The company has two sites: Leeds and Hull. The former is larger.
The company has three sites. The latter is larger.
The company has two sites: Leeds and Hull. The latter is larger.
The company has two sites; the second is larger.
exercises.explain: 'The latter' can only refer to the second of two items, not to one of three.

exercises.q: Repair the comma splice with a semicolon and a result adverb: 'The road was closed, we took the ferry.' → The road was closed; ___, we took the ferry.
exercises.explain: A result adverb after a semicolon links the two clauses correctly.
